learn.hook: Some numbers can be written as a neat fraction. Others, like √2, refuse to be caught by any fraction at all, no matter how hard you try!
points: A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Examples: 3 = 3/1, −0.5 = −1/2, 0 = 0/1.
Every natural number, whole number and integer is also a rational number.
An irrational number cannot be written as p/q. Examples: √2, √3, √5 and π.
If n is a natural number that is not a perfect square, then √n is irrational. But √16 = 4 is rational.
Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more rational numbers; their average is always one of them.

example.q: Find three rational numbers between 1/3 and 1/2.
steps: Multiply top and bottom by 2 to make room: 8/24 and 12/24

learn.reallife: The diagonal of a square tile of side 1 m is √2 m long. A carpenter can measure it closely, but never as an exact fraction!

games.title: Rational or irrational?

0.1010010001... (one more 0 each time)

games.title: True or false?
items: Every integer is a rational number
Any integer n can be written as n/1.
π is exactly equal to 22/7
22/7 is only a handy approximation. π is irrational, so no fraction equals it exactly.
The square root of every natural number is irrational
√9 = 3 and √25 = 5 are rational. Only non-perfect squares give irrational roots.
0 is a rational number
0 = 0/1, which is in the form p/q with q ≠ 0.
The sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational
√2 + (−√2) = 0, and 0 is rational.
3√2 is irrational
A non-zero rational number times an irrational number is always irrational.

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is irrational?
quiz.explain: 11 is not a perfect square, so √11 cannot be written as p/q. √25 = 5, 0.6 = 3/5 and −7/3 are all rational.
steps: √n is irrational if n is not a perfect square.
11 is not a perfect square, so √11 is irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every number with a root sign is irrational

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is rational?
quiz.explain: √36 = 6 = 6/1, which is rational. The others cannot be written as fractions.
steps: √12 (12 not a square), π and 3 + √5 are irrational.
quiz.mistake: Sees the root sign and assumes the number must be irrational

quiz.q: Which number lies between 2/5 and 3/5?
quiz.explain: 2/5 = 0.4 and 3/5 = 0.6. Their average is 1/2 = 0.5, which lies between them.
quiz.mistake: Compares only numerators or denominators instead of the whole fractions

quiz.q: Meena's calculator shows √2 = 1.414213562. Which statement is correct?
options: The display is only an approximation; √2 is irrational and its decimals never end or repeat
√2 is rational because the calculator shows a decimal
quiz.explain: √2 is irrational. A calculator can only show a few digits, so what you see is a rounded value.
steps: √2 is irrational: its decimals never end or repeat.
A calculator can show only a few digits.
So 1.414213562 is a rounded value, not exact.
Answer: The display is only an approximation; √2 is irrational and its decimals never end or repeat
quiz.mistake: Believes a calculator display is always exact

quiz.q: What kind of number is 2 + √3?
quiz.explain: A rational number plus an irrational number is always irrational. If 2 + √3 were p/q, then √3 would be p/q − 2, a fraction, which is impossible.
steps: Suppose 2 + √3 = p/q. Then √3 = p/q − 2, a fraction.
But √3 is irrational, so this is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding a whole number makes the result rational

quiz.q: What is √2 × √8?
quiz.explain: √2 × √8 = √(2 × 8) = √16 = 4. Two irrational numbers can multiply to give a rational one.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers under the root instead of multiplying them

quiz.q: How many rational numbers lie between 1 and 2?
quiz.explain: You can always find another rational number between any two, for example 1.5, 1.25, 1.125, ... so the list never ends.
steps: Between any two rationals there is another, e.g. their average.
quiz.mistake: Counts only decimals with one decimal place (1.1 to 1.9)

quiz.q: Which of these is a rational number even though it has a root sign?
quiz.explain: √(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4, which is rational.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every square root is irrational

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: "What is the difference between a rational and an irrational number? They both look like numbers to me!"
teach.praise: So a rational number can be written as a fraction p/q, and an irrational one like √2 or π never can. Clear as a blue sky!
teach.nudge: Can every number be written as a fraction? Can you give me an example that cannot?

revise.summary: A rational number can be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0; an irrational number cannot. √n is irrational when n is not a perfect square.
focus: Classify numbers as rational or irrational.
Find rational numbers between two rationals.
Know that rational + irrational is irrational.
traps: Not every number with a root sign is irrational.
A calculator display of √2 is only approximate.
Adding a whole number to an irrational does not make it rational.

learn.hook: ½, 2/4 and 50/100 look different, but they are the same slice of pizza!
points: Equivalent fractions name the same rational number: 2/3 = 4/6 = 10/15. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same non-zero number.
Lowest form: divide by the HCF so that p and q are co-prime (no common factor except 1). 18/24 = 3/4.
Add or subtract using a common denominator; multiply tops and bottoms; to divide, multiply by the reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).
Distributive property: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c and a × (b − c) = a × b − a × c also hold for rationals and can make calculations shorter.
learn.reallife: Recipes for 4 people scaled to 6 need fraction multiplication: ¾ cup × 6/4 = 9/8 cups.

quiz.explain: The HCF of 36 and 84 is 12.

quiz.explain: 15/−24: multiply −5 and 8 by −3 to get 15 and −24.
steps: Equivalent: multiply top and bottom by the same non-zero number.
−5/16 and 10/−8 change only one part; −8/5 is flipped.

quiz.explain: Common denominator 12: 10/12 − 9/12.

Drops the sign or cancels wrongly

quiz.explain: Multiply by the reciprocal: 4/9 × 3/2 = 12/18 = 2/3.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies straight across instead of using the reciprocal

quiz.mistake: Multiplies each pair and makes arithmetic slips

The others show associative, commutative or identity rules.

quiz.explain: Dividing 14 and 21 by 7 gives 2/3.

focus: Write equivalent fractions and lowest forms.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide rationals.

topics.title: Rationals on the number line and absolute value

learn.hook: How far is −3 from 0? Exactly as far as 3. Distance never goes negative!
points: To show p/q on the number line, divide each unit into q equal parts and count p parts from 0 (right for positive, left for negative). 7/4 = 1¾: go to 1, then 3 of the 4 parts.
The absolute value |a| is the distance of a from 0: |−5| = 5 and |5| = 5.
The distance between a and b on the line is |a − b|, e.g. between −2 and 3/2 it is |−2 − 3/2| = 7/2.
For a < b, the average (a + b)/2 lies between them: (a + b)/2 − a = (b − a)/2 > 0 and b − (a + b)/2 = (b − a)/2 > 0. It is exactly halfway.

example.q: Show that (a + b)/2 is between 1/3 and 1/2, and find it.

learn.reallife: The lift display at a mall shows −2 for the second basement; how many floors to go up to floor 3 is |3 − (−2)| = 5.

quiz.q: To mark 5/3 on the number line, how should each unit be divided?
quiz.explain: The denominator 3 tells how many equal parts each unit gets; then count 5 parts.
steps: To mark p/q, divide each unit into q equal parts.
For 5/3, q = 3; then count 5 parts from 0.
quiz.mistake: Divides by the numerator instead of the denominator

quiz.q: Between which two integers does −11/4 lie?
quiz.explain: −11/4 = −2.75, which is between −3 and −2.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the sign or rounds the wrong way

quiz.q: What is |−17|?
quiz.explain: Absolute value is distance from 0, never negative.
steps: |a| is the distance of a from 0.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the minus sign

quiz.mistake: Subtracts the sizes, getting 3

quiz.q: What is the distance between −5/6 and 1/3?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts without changing the sign of −5/6

quiz.q: What is the average of −2 and 6, and where does it lie?
quiz.explain: (−2 + 6)/2 = 2. Its distance from each end is 4.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding before halving

quiz.q: For a < b, why is (a + b)/2 always bigger than a?
options: Because (a + b)/2 − a = (b − a)/2, which is positive
quiz.explain: b − a > 0, so half of it is also positive.
steps: a < b, so b − a > 0, and half of it is positive.
So (a + b)/2 > a, whatever the signs of a and b.
Answer: Because (a + b)/2 − a = (b − a)/2, which is positive
quiz.mistake: Assumes the numbers are positive

quiz.q: Which point is farther from 0: −3/2 or 5/4?
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative numbers are always closer to 0

teach.praise: Spot on! Absolute value is distance from zero, and −2 to 5 is 7 apart!
teach.nudge: What does absolute value measure? How can you find the gap between two numbers?

revise.summary: To show p/q on the line, split each unit into q parts and count p. |a| is distance from 0, and the distance between a and b is |a − b|. The average lies exactly halfway.
focus: Mark rationals on the number line.
Find absolute values and distances.
Show the average lies between two numbers.
traps: Divide each unit by the denominator, not the numerator.
Absolute value is never negative.
Subtracting a negative means adding.

learn.hook: Between 1/2 and 3/4 there's always another fraction, and between those another... forever!
points: The rational numbers are dense: between any two rationals there are infinitely many more.
Method 1, averages: (a + b)/2 is between a and b; repeat with the new pairs.
Method 2, common denominators: write both with a bigger common denominator, e.g. 3/5 = 30/50 and 4/5 = 40/50, then 31/50, 32/50, ..., 39/50 are between them.
Method 3, extra decimal places: between 0.3 and 0.4 lie 0.31, 0.32, ..., and between 0.31 and 0.32 lie 0.311, 0.312, ...
To find exactly n rationals between two numbers, scale up the denominators until there are at least n numerators in between.

example.q: Find five rational numbers between 2/3 and 3/4.

learn.reallife: Petrol prices like ₹102.345 per litre and ₹102.346 per litre show there is always a finer value in between.

Use decimals to find rationals between.

Don't add tops and bottoms to find a fraction between.

To solve an equation with fractions, multiply both sides by the LCM of the denominators to clear them, then solve as usual.

Find leftovers.
Solve equations with fractions.

learn.hook: The diagonal of a 1 m square tile cannot be written as any fraction at all. Here's the proof!
points: The diagonal of a unit square has length √2 (by Pythagoras, 1² + 1² = 2). No fraction p/q has square exactly 2.
Proof by contradiction (linked to Hippasus): suppose √2 = p/q in lowest form. Then p² = 2q², so p² is even, so p is even: p = 2k.
Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k², so q is even too. Both even contradicts 'lowest form', so √2 is irrational.
The same idea works for √3, √5 and √p for any prime p: if p divides a², then p divides a.
For √5: assume √5 = a/b in lowest terms; a² = 5b², so 5 divides a; write a = 5c; then 25c² = 5b², b² = 5c², so 5 divides b. Contradiction.

example.q: In the proof that √3 is irrational, why does a² = 3b² mean 3 divides a?
steps: If a prime divides a square, it divides the number itself
example.answer: Because 3 is prime, 3 | a² gives 3 | a

learn.reallife: Tile-setters cutting a square tile diagonally use √2 ≈ 1.414 times the side, knowing the exact value never ends.

games.title: Proof that √2 is irrational
items: Assume √2 = p/q in lowest form
Square: p² = 2q², so p is even
Write p = 2k, so q² = 2k²
So q is even too
Contradiction: p/q was not in lowest form

games.title: Proof check
items: If p² is even then p is even.
An odd number squared is odd, so p cannot be odd.
The proof assumes p/q is in lowest form.
The contradiction is that both turn out even.
The same proof shows √4 is irrational.
√4 = 2; the step 'if 4 divides a² then 4 divides a' fails (a = 2).
If 5 divides a², then 5 divides a.
5 is prime.
The diagonal of a unit square is 2.
It is √2.

quiz.q: What is the length of the diagonal of a square of side 1 m?

steps: Diagonal d of a 1 m square: d² = 1² + 1² = 2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of using Pythagoras

quiz.q: A proof by contradiction starts by:
options: assuming what you want to prove
assuming the opposite of what you want to prove
quiz.explain: You assume √2 is rational and show that this leads to something impossible.
steps: Proof by contradiction assumes the opposite.
To prove √2 irrational, assume √2 is rational.
Then show this leads to something impossible.
Answer: assuming the opposite of what you want to prove
quiz.mistake: Thinks a proof checks examples

quiz.q: In the proof that √2 is irrational, from p² = 2q² we conclude:
quiz.explain: p² is twice a whole number, so it is even; only even numbers have even squares.
steps: p² = 2q² is twice a whole number, so p² is even.
Only even numbers have even squares.
quiz.mistake: Concludes about q before p

quiz.q: After writing p = 2k, the equation p² = 2q² becomes:
quiz.explain: (2k)² = 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the 2 in 2k

quiz.q: What is the contradiction at the end of the √2 proof?
options: p and q are both even, but p/q was in lowest form
quiz.explain: Lowest form means no common factor, yet both share the factor 2.
steps: p/q was chosen in lowest form: no common factor.
The proof shows p and q are both even.
Both sharing factor 2 contradicts lowest form.
Answer: p and q are both even, but p/q was in lowest form
quiz.mistake: Does not see why both being even is a problem

quiz.q: For √5 = a/b in lowest form, a² = 5b². Writing a = 5c gives:
quiz.explain: 25c² = 5b², so b² = 5c², which means 5 divides b as well.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 25 instead of 5

quiz.q: Which key fact makes the √p proof work for a prime p?
options: Every number has a square root
If p divides a², then p divides a
quiz.explain: For primes this is true; it is what forces both a and b to share the factor p.
steps: The key step: if prime p divides a², then p divides a.
This forces both a and b to share the factor p.
Answer: If p divides a², then p divides a
quiz.mistake: Thinks the proof works for any number, prime or not

quiz.q: Why does the same argument NOT prove √9 is irrational?
options: Because the proof only works for 2
quiz.explain: 9 divides a² does not force 9 to divide a (e.g. a = 3). And indeed √9 = 3 is rational.
steps: 9 is a perfect square: √9 = 3, which is rational.
Also 9 is not prime: 9 | a² does not force 9 | a (try a = 3).
Answer: Because 9 is a perfect square: √9 = 3
quiz.mistake: Applies the proof blindly to every square root

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can anyone prove √2 is not a fraction?"
teach.praise: Amazing! Assume it's a fraction in lowest form, show both parts are even, contradiction!
teach.nudge: How does the proof begin? What goes wrong with p and q?

revise.summary: √2 is irrational: assuming √2 = p/q in lowest form forces p and q to both be even, a contradiction. The same proof works for √p when p is prime.
focus: Write the proof that √2 is irrational.
Adapt it for √3 or √5.
Know why it fails for perfect squares.
remember: p² = 2q² → p even → p = 2k → q² = 2k² → q even: contradiction.
Key fact: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a.
traps: Conclude about p before q.
(2k)² = 4k², not 2k².
The proof does not apply to √9 = 3.

learn.hook: √2 is not a fraction, yet you can mark it exactly on a number line with just a ruler and a compass. Here is the trick!
points: Rational and irrational numbers together make up the real numbers.
Every real number is a point on the number line, and every point on the line is a real number. The line has no gaps.
To mark √2: draw a right triangle on the line with legs 1 and 1. Its hypotenuse is √(1 + 1) = √2; swing an arc from 0 with that length.
In the same way, legs 2 and 1 give √5, and legs √2 and 1 give √3.
To compare roots, compare squares: √10 < 3.2 because 10 < 3.2² = 10.24.

example.q: Show how to mark √5 on the number line.
steps: Mark O at 0 and A at 2 on the number line
At A, draw AB = 1 unit perpendicular to the line
With centre O and radius OB, draw an arc to cut the line at P. Then OP = √5 ≈ 2.24
example.answer: P is the point √5, a little to the right of 2.2

learn.reallife: A ruler with marks only at whole and half centimetres still contains the point √2 cm: every length you can draw is a real number.

quiz.q: Between which two whole numbers does √20 lie?
quiz.explain: 4² = 16 and 5² = 25. Since 16 < 20 < 25, √20 lies between 4 and 5.
quiz.mistake: Looks at numbers near 20 instead of the squares near 20

quiz.q: To mark √2 on the number line, which right triangle do you draw?
quiz.explain: With legs 1 and 1 the hypotenuse is √(1² + 1²) = √2.
quiz.mistake: Uses legs 1 and 2, which give √5 instead

quiz.q: Which is greater, √10 or 3.2?
quiz.explain: Compare squares: (√10)² = 10 and 3.2² = 10.24. Since 10 < 10.24, 3.2 is greater.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number with a root sign must be bigger, or guesses √10 ≈ 3.3

quiz.q: From 0 on a number line, Arjun marks 3 units, draws a 2-unit perpendicular there and swings the hypotenuse down onto the line. Which number does he get?
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse is √(3² + 2²) = √(9 + 4) = √13.
quiz.mistake: Adds the legs (5) or forgets to take the square root (13)

quiz.q: Which statement about the number line is true?
options: Only rational numbers can be marked on it
√2 cannot be shown on it because its decimals never end
Every point on it stands for a real number
There are gaps that no number fills
quiz.explain: The real numbers fill the whole line: each point is a real number and each real number has a point.
steps: Rationals and irrationals together are the real numbers.
Every point on the line is a real number, and the line has no gaps.
√2 can be marked using a right triangle.
Answer: Every point on it stands for a real number
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number must have a finite decimal to have a place on the line

quiz.q: Which list is in increasing order?
quiz.mistake: Thinks √2 is bigger than 1.5

quiz.q: Riya jumps √9 units and then √16 more units to the right of 0. Where does she land?
quiz.explain: √9 = 3 and √16 = 4, so she lands at 3 + 4 = 7. Note that √9 + √16 is not the same as √(9 + 16) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Writes √9 + √16 = √25 = 5, adding under one root

quiz.q: √50 is closest to which value?
quiz.explain: 7² = 49, so √50 is just a little more than 7. In fact 7.07² ≈ 49.98.
quiz.mistake: Halves the number instead of taking its square root

teach.ask: Gappu holds a compass: "How can I put √2 on a number line if I can't even write it as a fraction?"
teach.praise: A right triangle with sides 1 and 1, then swing the hypotenuse down with a compass. √2 has a home on the line!
teach.nudge: What shape do I draw first, and how do I bring its long side down onto the line?

revise.summary: Rationals and irrationals together form the real numbers, which fill the number line with no gaps. √2, √3 and √5 can be marked using right triangles.
focus: Mark √2, √3 and √5 on the number line.
Compare roots by comparing squares.
Know that every point is a real number.
remember: Legs 1 and 1 → √2; legs 2 and 1 → √5; legs √2 and 1 → √3.
traps: Legs 1 and 2 give √5, not √2.
A number does not need a finite decimal to have a place on the line.

topics.title: The square-root spiral, π and the journey of numbers

learn.hook: A spiral of right triangles draws √2, √3, √4, √5 ... one after another like a snail shell!
points: Square-root spiral: start with a right triangle with legs 1 and 1 (hypotenuse √2). On that hypotenuse put a new leg of 1 at right angles: the new hypotenuse is √3, then √4 = 2, √5, and so on.
π, the ratio of circumference to diameter, is irrational. Aryabhata gave the approximation 62832/20000 = 3927/1250 = 3.1416.
Madhava of Sangamagrama found the infinite series π = 4(1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + ...).
Number systems grew by need: N (counting) → Z (debts, zero) → Q (sharing) → irrationals (lengths like √2) → R (the whole number line).
A teaser: no real number squared is negative, so mathematicians later invented i = √(−1), the start of complex numbers.

example.q: In the square-root spiral, what is the hypotenuse of the 7th triangle?

learn.reallife: Space agencies use π to many decimal places for orbits, but Aryabhata's 3.1416 is already accurate to 4 decimal places.

games.title: How number systems grew
items: Natural numbers N
Integers Z
Rational numbers Q
Irrational numbers
Real numbers R

quiz.q: In the square-root spiral, the hypotenuse after √5 is:
quiz.explain: Each new triangle adds a leg of 1: (√5)² + 1² = 6.
steps: Each new triangle adds a leg of 1 to the last hypotenuse.
quiz.mistake: Squares the previous hypotenuse length incorrectly

quiz.q: Which hypotenuse in the spiral is a whole number?
quiz.explain: √9 = 3. (√4 = 2 and √16 = 4 are the others.)
steps: √n is whole only when n is a perfect square.
quiz.mistake: Thinks no hypotenuse can be whole

quiz.q: Aryabhata's value of π is 3927/1250. What is it as a decimal?
quiz.explain: 3927 ÷ 1250 = 3.1416, and π = 3.14159... so this is correct to four decimal places.
steps: Answer: 3.1416, correct to four decimal places
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with 22/7 ≈ 3.1428

quiz.q: What are the first three terms inside Madhava's series for π?
quiz.explain: The series uses odd denominators with alternating signs, all multiplied by 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses all whole numbers instead of odd numbers

quiz.q: Using just the first three terms, 4(1 − 1/3 + 1/5) = ?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by 4

quiz.q: Is π rational or irrational?
quiz.explain: π's decimals never end and never repeat; 22/7 = 3.142857... is close but not equal.
steps: π's decimals never end and never repeat, so π is irrational.
Answer: Irrational; 22/7 is only an approximation
quiz.mistake: Thinks 22/7 is the exact value of π

quiz.q: Which number system was needed to answer 'what is 3 − 5?'
quiz.explain: 3 − 5 = −2 needs negative numbers, which the integers include.
steps: Natural numbers have no negatives; integers do.
quiz.mistake: Thinks natural numbers include negatives

quiz.q: Why is i = √(−1) not a real number?
options: Because square roots are always irrational
No real number squared gives a negative number
quiz.explain: Every real number squared is 0 or positive, so √(−1) needs a new kind of number.
steps: Any real number squared is 0 or positive.
So no real number has square −1.
√(−1) needs a new kind of number, i.
Answer: No real number squared gives a negative number
quiz.mistake: Thinks √(−1) = −1

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How did we go from counting numbers to real numbers?"
teach.praise: Beautiful! Counting, then negatives, fractions, irrationals, and finally all reals!
teach.nudge: What came after natural numbers? What kind of number is √2?

revise.summary: The square-root spiral builds √2, √3, √4, ... by adding legs of 1. π is irrational; Aryabhata gave 3.1416 and Madhava an infinite series. Number systems grew by need, from N to R.
focus: Find hypotenuses in the square-root spiral.
Know Aryabhata's and Madhava's work on π.
Trace N → Z → Q → R and why i is not real.
remember: No real number squared is negative, so i = √(−1) is not real.
traps: 22/7 is not the exact value of π.
Madhava's series uses odd denominators, not all whole numbers.

learn.hook: Divide 1 by 8 and the division stops. Divide 1 by 7 and the digits 142857 go round and round forever. Why?
points: The decimal expansion of a rational number either terminates (ends), like 3/8 = 0.375, or is non-terminating and recurring (repeats), like 1/3 = 0.333...
A fraction in lowest terms terminates only if its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 7/20 terminates, but 5/12 repeats.
An irrational number has a decimal expansion that is non-terminating and non-recurring: it never ends and never settles into a repeating block.
A repeating decimal can be turned back into p/q. For 0.777..., let x = 0.777...; then 10x = 7.777..., so 9x = 7 and x = 7/9.
The repeating block is shown with a bar on top, for example 0.27 with a bar on 27 means 0.272727...

example.q: Write 0.474747... (47 repeating) in the form p/q.
steps: Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100: 100x = 47.474747...

learn.reallife: When ₹100 is shared equally among 3 friends, each share is ₹33.333..., so in real life we round it to ₹33.33.

games.title: What kind of decimal?
items: π

items.q: 0.454545... (45 repeating) as a fraction in lowest terms

quiz.q: What is the decimal expansion of 7/8?
quiz.explain: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875. The division ends because 8 = 2³ has only the prime factor 2.
quiz.mistake: Just writes the numerator and denominator side by side after the point

quiz.q: Which fraction has a terminating decimal expansion?
quiz.explain: 40 = 2³ × 5 has only 2s and 5s, so 11/40 = 0.275 terminates. 7, 12 = 2² × 3 and 9 = 3² all contain other primes.
steps: Terminates only if the denominator (lowest form) has primes 2 and 5 only.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an even denominator always gives a terminating decimal

quiz.q: The decimal expansion of an irrational number is:
quiz.explain: If the decimal ended or repeated, the number could be written as p/q and would be rational.
steps: If an irrational's decimal ended or repeated, it could be written as p/q.
So its decimal never ends and never repeats.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any decimal that goes on forever is irrational, even if it repeats

quiz.q: Write 0.777... (7 repeating) as a fraction.
quiz.explain: Let x = 0.777...; 10x = 7.777...; subtracting gives 9x = 7, so x = 7/9.
quiz.mistake: Writes 7/10, treating the repeating decimal as if it stopped after one digit

quiz.q: Write 0.363636... (36 repeating) in lowest terms.
quiz.explain: Two digits repeat: 100x − x = 36, so x = 36/99 = 4/11.
quiz.mistake: Uses 90 instead of 99 when two digits repeat

quiz.q: 1/7 = 0.142857142857... How many digits are in its repeating block?
quiz.explain: The block 142857 repeats, and it has 6 digits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the block length must equal the denominator 7

quiz.q: Aisha shares ₹100 equally among 3 friends. Which describes 100/3 as a decimal?
quiz.explain: 100 ÷ 3 = 33.333..., with 3 repeating forever. It repeats, so it is rational, not irrational.
steps: 100 ÷ 3 = 33 remainder 1, and each further step gives 3 again.
A repeating decimal is rational, not irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rounded money value is the exact answer

quiz.q: Which number is irrational?
quiz.explain: In 0.1211211121111... the number of 1s keeps growing, so no fixed block repeats. It never ends and never repeats, so it is irrational.
steps: 0.1212... repeats, 0.125 terminates, 12/99 is a fraction: all rational.
In 0.1211211121111... the number of 1s keeps growing.
No block repeats and it never ends, so it is irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any long decimal is irrational without checking for a repeating block

teach.ask: Gappu taps the calculator: "Some decimals stop, some repeat and some go wild. How can I tell which numbers are rational from their decimals?"
teach.praise: Decimals that end or repeat belong to rational numbers; decimals that never end and never repeat are irrational. Tweet-tastic!
teach.nudge: What happens to the decimal of 1/3 compared with √2? Does one of them repeat?

revise.summary: A rational number's decimal either terminates or repeats; an irrational's never ends and never repeats. A fraction in lowest form terminates only if its denominator has only 2s and 5s.
focus: Decide if a fraction terminates or repeats.
Convert repeating decimals to p/q.
Identify irrational decimals.
traps: An even denominator does not guarantee termination: 5/12 repeats.
A decimal that goes on forever but repeats is rational.
Use 99 when two digits repeat, not 90.

topics.title: Decimals to fractions and cyclic numbers

learn.hook: 1/7 hides a magic number: 142857. Multiply it by 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 and the same digits just rotate!
points: If p/q in lowest form has q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ, the decimal ends after the larger of m and n places: 7/40 = 7/(2³ × 5) has 3 places (0.175).
Terminating decimal to fraction: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8.
Repeating decimal: if x = 0.4545..., 100x = 45.4545..., so 99x = 45 and x = 5/11. For a mixed repeating decimal like 0.1666..., use 10x = 1.666... and 100x = 16.666...; then 90x = 15, x = 1/6.
0.999... = 1: if x = 0.999..., then 10x = 9.999..., so 9x = 9 and x = 1. Some numbers have two decimal forms.
1/7 = 0.142857..., and 2/7, 3/7, ..., 6/7 use the same six digits rotated (2/7 = 0.285714...). The fractions k/13 split into two such rotating families: 076923 and 153846.

example.q: Write 0.2333... (3 repeating) as a fraction.

learn.reallife: Bank interest rates like 7.5% per year are terminating decimals because their denominators are made of 2s and 5s.

quiz.q: How many decimal places does 13/80 have?
quiz.explain: 80 = 2⁴ × 5. The larger power is 4, so 4 places: 13/80 = 0.1625.
quiz.mistake: Counts the number of digits in the denominator

quiz.q: Write 0.64 as a fraction in lowest form.
quiz.mistake: Reduces only part way

quiz.q: Write 0.272727... (27 repeating) as a fraction in lowest form.
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 as the denominator, as for a terminating decimal

quiz.q: Write 0.8333... (3 repeating) as a fraction.
quiz.mistake: Treats it as a pure repeating decimal

quiz.q: Using x = 0.999..., what does 10x − x give?
quiz.explain: 10x = 9.999..., and subtracting x removes all the 9s after the point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 0.999... must be less than 1

quiz.q: 1/7 = 0.142857... What is 3/7 as a decimal?
quiz.explain: 3/7 uses the same digits rotated, starting from 4: 0.428571...
steps: k/7 uses the six digits of 142857 rotated.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 3/7 is 3 times each digit separately

quiz.q: What is 142857 × 7?
quiz.mistake: Expects the answer to be a rotation of 142857

quiz.q: 1/13 = 0.076923... Which of these is a rotation of 076923 and so belongs to the same family?
quiz.explain: 769230 is 076923 rotated. 2/13, 5/13 and 7/13 belong to the other family, 153846.
steps: 153846, 384615 and 538461 belong to the other family.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every k/13 uses the same six digits

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I turn 0.444... into a fraction?"
teach.praise: Super! Let x be the decimal, multiply by 10, subtract, and solve: 4/9!
teach.nudge: What do you multiply x by? What do you do with the two equations?

revise.summary: If q = 2ᵐ × 5ⁿ, p/q ends after the larger of m and n places. Repeating decimals convert to fractions by multiplying and subtracting; 0.999... = 1; sevenths and thirteenths form cyclic families.
focus: Convert terminating and repeating decimals to fractions.
Handle mixed repeating decimals.
Use cyclic patterns of 1/7 and 1/13.
traps: 0.999... is not less than 1.
A mixed repeating decimal needs 10x and 100x, not just 100x.
Not every k/13 uses the same six digits.

learn.hook: 4² − 3² = 7, 5² − 4² = 9, 6² − 5² = 11... odd numbers keep popping out. Why? Draw squares and see!
points: Number patterns hint at identities: (n + 1)² − n² is always 2n + 1, the odd number n + (n + 1).
(a + b)²: a square of side a + b splits into an a × a square, a b × b square and two a × b rectangles, so it equals a² + 2ab + b².
(a − b)²: from the a × a square cut off two a × b strips (they overlap in a b × b square, which gets removed twice), so add b² back: a² − 2ab + b².
(a + b)(a − b): cut a b × b square from an a × a square and rearrange the L-shape into an (a + b) × (a − b) rectangle, so it equals a² − b².
(x + a)(x + b): a rectangle of sides x + a and x + b splits into x², ax, bx and ab, so it equals x² + (a + b)x + ab.

example.q: A square of side (x + 3) is split into pieces. List their areas and the total.

learn.reallife: Tilers covering a square floor with a border find the tile count using exactly these area splits.

games.title: Area model check
items: A square of side a + b contains two a × b rectangles.
That is where 2ab comes from.
The area of an (x + 4) × (x + 1) rectangle is x² + 4x + 4.
It is x² + 5x + 4.
In the (a − b)² model, the b × b corner is removed twice, so b² is added back.
That gives a² − 2ab + b².
(a + b)² = a² + b².
The two rectangles 2ab are missing.

quiz.mistake: Thinks consecutive squares differ by 1

quiz.q: A square of side (a + b) is cut into 4 pieces. Which list gives their areas?
quiz.explain: A side split into a and b gives an a × a square, a b × b square and two a × b rectangles.
steps: Split each side of the (a + b) square into a and b.
Pieces: an a × a square, a b × b square and two a × b rectangles.
Areas: a², b², ab, ab (total a² + 2ab + b²).

quiz.mistake: Subtracts 2ab but forgets to add b² back

quiz.explain: The pieces are x², 3x, 5x and 15. 3x + 5x = 8x.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only the first terms and the last terms

quiz.q: In the area model of (x + a)(x + b), which piece gives the constant term ab?
quiz.explain: The rectangle made from the parts a and b has area ab.
steps: (x + a)(x + b) splits into x², ax, bx and ab.
The piece with sides a and b has area ab, the constant term.
Answer: The small a × b rectangle
quiz.mistake: Thinks the constant comes from the big square

quiz.q: Which identity does the pattern 3² − 2² = 5, 4² − 3² = 7, 5² − 4² = 9 come from?
quiz.explain: The difference of consecutive squares is always the next odd number 2n + 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 2n part of the expansion

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Why is (a + b)² not just a² + b²? Show me with a picture!"
teach.praise: Lovely! The big square has two extra a × b rectangles, so 2ab!
teach.nudge: Draw a square of side a + b. What pieces do you see apart from a² and b²?

revise.summary: Area models show why identities work: a square of side a + b splits into a², b² and two ab rectangles, and cutting and rearranging shapes gives (a − b)² and a² − b².
focus: Explain each identity with an area picture.
Use area models to expand expressions.
Spot identities from number patterns.
traps: Don't forget the two ab rectangles.
In (a − b)², the b² square is removed twice, so add it back.
Consecutive squares differ by 2n + 1, not 1.

learn.hook: Can you find 103 × 103 in your head in five seconds? With the right identity, you can!
points: An identity is an equality that is true for every value of the variables, unlike an equation such as x + 2 = 5, which is true for only one value.
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Picture a square of side a + b split into an a × a square, a b × b square and two a × b rectangles.
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
(x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.

example.q: Find 103² without long multiplication.
steps: 103 = 100 + 3, so use (a + b)² with a = 100, b = 3

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers who multiply mentally often use these tricks: 49 × 51 = 50² − 1² = 2499.

steps: Use (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² with a = x, b = 7.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the middle term 2ab and writes x² + 49

quiz.q: Use (a − b)² to find 98².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the middle term (getting 9804) or drops the + b² (getting 9600)

quiz.q: Expand (3a − 2b)².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the middle term, writing 6ab

quiz.explain: Use (x + a)(x + b) with a = 4, b = −9: a + b = −5 and ab = −36.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of the middle term wrong

quiz.q: If a + b = 10 and ab = 21, find a² + b².

quiz.mistake: Takes a² + b² = (a + b)², forgetting the 2ab

quiz.q: Which of these is an identity (true for every value of x)?
quiz.explain: (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1 holds for every x. The others are true only for some values (or are false in general).
steps: An identity is true for every value of x.
Test x = 1: (x + 1)² = x² + 1 gives 4 = 2 ✗; x + 1 = 5 and 2x = x² fail too.
(x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1 is (a + b)² with a = x, b = 1.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an equation that is true for one value with an identity

quiz.mistake: Uses only a − b and forgets to multiply by a + b

teach.ask: Gappu groans: "Why isn't (a + b)² just a² + b²? That looks so much simpler!"
teach.praise: Of course! The big square also has two a × b rectangles, so (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² for every value. I won't forget 2ab now!
teach.nudge: If you draw a square of side a + b, what pieces do you see besides a² and b²?

revise.summary: An identity is true for every value of its variables. The key ones are (a ± b)², (a + b)(a − b) and (x + a)(x + b); they also speed up arithmetic.
focus: Expand using the standard identities.
Use identities for quick calculations.
Tell an identity from an equation.
remember: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
traps: (a + b)² is not a² + b²: don't drop 2ab.
Double the middle term.
An equation true for one value is not an identity.

learn.hook: Expanding is like opening a gift box; factorising is packing it back. Identities show you how the box was folded!
points: To factorise means to write an expression as a product of simpler expressions.
Always take out a common factor first: 3x² − 75 = 3(x² − 25).
Look for patterns: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²; a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)².
For x² + px + q, find two numbers with sum p and product q: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4).
a³ + b³ and a³ − b³ have their own factor forms. Always check by expanding your answer.

example.q: Factorise 4x² − 12x + 9.
steps: Middle term: 2 × 2x × 3 = 12x, with a minus sign
So it matches a² − 2ab + b² with a = 2x, b = 3

learn.reallife: If a rectangular rangoli has area x² + 9x + 20, factorising tells you possible side lengths: (x + 4) and (x + 5).

games.title: Match each expression with its factors
Factorise 3x² − 75
items: Take out the common factor 3: 3(x² − 25)
Spot a difference of squares: x² − 5²
Use a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)
Write the answer 3(x − 5)(x + 5)

quiz.q: Factorise 9y² − 16.
quiz.explain: 9y² − 16 = (3y)² − 4², a difference of squares.
steps: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) with a = 3y, b = 4.
quiz.mistake: Writes a difference of squares as a perfect square

quiz.q: Factorise x² + 8x + 16.
steps: Matches a² + 2ab + b² with a = x, b = 4.
quiz.mistake: Finds numbers with product 16 but ignores the sum 8

quiz.q: Factorise x² − 7x + 12.
quiz.explain: We need two numbers with sum −7 and product 12: −3 and −4.
quiz.mistake: Uses + signs even though the middle term is negative

quiz.q: Factorise 2x² − 18 completely.
quiz.explain: Take out 2 to get 2(x² − 9), then x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3).
quiz.mistake: Stops after taking out the common factor

quiz.q: Use factorisation to find 87² − 13².
quiz.mistake: Computes (87 − 13)² = 5476 instead

quiz.q: Factorise x² + x − 20.
quiz.explain: Two numbers with product −20 and sum +1 are 5 and −4.
quiz.mistake: Puts the signs the wrong way round, giving a sum of −1

quiz.q: Factorise 27a³ − 8.
steps: a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) with a → 3a, b → 2.
quiz.mistake: Uses a minus sign in the second bracket, mixing it up with a³ + b³

quiz.q: A rectangular rangoli has area x² + 9x + 20 square units. One side is (x + 4). What is the other side?
steps: Find two numbers with sum 9 and product 20: 4 and 5.
One side is (x + 4), so the other is (x + 5).
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 4 from 20 instead of dividing, or uses the coefficient 9

teach.ask: Gappu stares at x² − 49: "How do I break this into factors? Where do I start?"
teach.praise: First take out anything common, then match a pattern like a² − b², and finally multiply back to check. x² − 49 = (x − 7)(x + 7)!
teach.nudge: Is 49 a square number? Which identity has a minus sign between two squares?

revise.summary: To factorise, write an expression as a product. Take out common factors first, then use identity patterns or find two numbers with the right sum and product.
focus: Factorise using a² − b², (a ± b)² and cube patterns.
Factorise x² + px + q.
Check by expanding.
traps: Don't stop after taking out the common factor.
A difference of squares is not a perfect square.
a³ − b³ has + ab in the second bracket; a³ + b³ has − ab.

topics.title: Fraction squares, three-term squares and reciprocals

learn.hook: x + 1/x = 3? Then x² + 1/x² is exactly 7, and you never need to know x!
points: Perfect squares can have fractional coefficients: x² + x + 1/4 = (x + 1/2)² because 2 × x × 1/2 = x.
A six-term expression may be a three-term square: x² + 4y² + 9z² + 4xy + 12yz + 6zx = (x + 2y + 3z)². Find the square roots of the squared terms and check the cross terms.
(x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x², so x² + 1/x² = (x + 1/x)² − 2. Similarly x² + 1/x² = (x − 1/x)² + 2.
'A number plus its reciprocal is k' gives x + 1/x = k, which becomes the quadratic x² − kx + 1 = 0 after multiplying by x.

example.q: A number plus its reciprocal is 10/3. Find the number.

learn.reallife: Engineers simplify formulas with fractions by spotting perfect squares, just as you will here.

items.text: (a + b + c)² has ___ terms when expanded
If x + 1/x = 4, then x² + 1/x² = ___

quiz.q: Factorise x² + (2/3)x + 1/9.
quiz.mistake: Takes the square root of the middle coefficient

quiz.q: Expand (y/2 − 2)².
steps: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² with a = y/2, b = 2.
quiz.mistake: Halves the middle term twice

quiz.q: Which expression equals (a + 2b + c)²?
quiz.explain: Square each term and add twice each product: 2(a)(2b) = 4ab, 2(2b)(c) = 4bc, 2(c)(a) = 2ca.
steps: (a + b + c)² rule with terms a, 2b, c.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the coefficient 2 in 2b

quiz.q: Factorise 4x² + y² + 9z² + 4xy + 6yz + 12zx.
quiz.explain: Square roots of the squares are 2x, y, 3z. Check: 2(2x)(y) = 4xy, 2(y)(3z) = 6yz, 2(3z)(2x) = 12zx.
quiz.mistake: Uses the squared coefficients instead of their square roots

quiz.q: If x + 1/x = 7, find x² + 1/x².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract 2, or adds it

quiz.q: If x − 1/x = 5, find x² + 1/x².
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 2 instead of adding

quiz.q: A number plus its reciprocal equals 5/2. Which numbers can it be?
quiz.mistake: Takes the given sum as the number

quiz.q: If a + b + c = 10 and a² + b² + c² = 38, find ab + bc + ca.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to halve

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If x + 1/x = 3, how can I find x² + 1/x² without finding x?"
teach.praise: Clever! Square both sides and subtract 2 to get 7!
teach.nudge: What happens if you square x + 1/x? What extra number appears?

revise.summary: Perfect squares can have fractions or three terms. (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x² gives x² + 1/x² from x + 1/x.
focus: Factorise squares with fractional coefficients.
Recognise three-term squares.
Use x + 1/x and x − 1/x to find x² + 1/x².
traps: Use square roots of the squared terms, not the coefficients.
Subtract 2 for x + 1/x; add 2 for x − 1/x.
Square the coefficient too: (2b)² = 4b².

learn.hook: 11³ = 1331 and 101³ = 1030301. Patterns like these come straight from the cube identities!
points: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b) = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³.
(a − b)³ = a³ − b³ − 3ab(a − b) = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³.
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) and a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca). So if a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.

example.q: Find 11³ using (a + b)³.

learn.reallife: Volumes of cube-shaped boxes grow as a cube. If each side of a 10 cm box grows by 1 cm, (a + b)³ shows exactly how much extra space you get.

games.title: Cube check
items: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³
You also need the term 3ab(a + b). Try a = b = 1: 8 is not 2.
a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)
Multiply out the right side and the middle terms cancel, leaving a³ − b³.
If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
This follows from a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(...), which is 0 when a + b + c = 0.
(a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c²
The cross terms 2ab + 2bc + 2ca are missing.
Use (a − b)³ = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³ with a = x, b = 1.

items.text: (a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + ___
(x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + ___

quiz.q: Expand (x + 2)³.
quiz.explain: a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³ with a = x, b = 2 gives x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.
quiz.mistake: Cubes each term separately and drops the middle terms

quiz.q: Find 102³ using an identity.
quiz.mistake: Uses 3ab instead of 3ab(a + b), getting 1000608, or forgets the middle part entirely

quiz.q: Find (−12)³ + 7³ + 5³ without cubing each number.
quiz.explain: −12 + 7 + 5 = 0, so the sum of cubes equals 3abc = 3 × (−12) × 7 × 5 = −1260.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the answer is 0 because a + b + c = 0, or drops the negative sign

quiz.q: Expand (x + y + 2)².
quiz.explain: Use a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca with c = 2: 2bc = 4y and 2ca = 4x.
steps: (a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca with a = x, b = y, c = 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the cross terms

quiz.q: Factorise x³ − 27.
quiz.explain: a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) with a = x, b = 3.
steps: a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) with a = x, b = 3.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the signs of the sum-of-cubes and difference-of-cubes identities

quiz.q: If x + y = 5 and xy = 6, find x³ + y³.
quiz.mistake: Thinks x³ + y³ = (x + y)³

quiz.q: Expand (2x − 1)³.
quiz.explain: (a − b)³ = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³ with a = 2x, b = 1: 8x³ − 12x² + 6x − 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to cube the 2 in 2x, or gets the alternating signs wrong

quiz.q: If a + b + c = 9 and ab + bc + ca = 26, find a² + b² + c².
quiz.explain: a² + b² + c² = (a + b + c)² − 2(ab + bc + ca) = 81 − 52 = 29.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 26 instead of 2 × 26

teach.ask: Gappu counts on his feathers: "Why does (a + b)³ have so many terms? Can't I just cube a and cube b?"
teach.praise: (a + b)³ is (a + b) multiplied three times, so the extra terms 3a²b + 3ab² appear. Just a³ + b³ is not enough!
teach.nudge: What do you get if you multiply (a + b)² by (a + b) once more?

revise.summary: Cube identities: (a ± b)³, a³ ± b³ and a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc. If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.
focus: Expand (a + b)³ and (a − b)³.
Factorise sums and differences of cubes.
Use the a + b + c = 0 shortcut.
traps: x³ + y³ is not (x + y)³.
Use 3ab(a + b), not just 3ab.
Double every cross term in (a + b + c)².

topics.title: More cube identities and testing identities

learn.hook: Is (a + b)³ the same as a³ + b³? Try a = b = 1: 8 versus 2. One test is enough to bust a fake identity!
points: Sum of cubes: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²).
x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx).
To use it with only x + y + z and xy + yz + zx known, first find x² + y² + z² = (x + y + z)² − 2(xy + yz + zx).
Verify an identity by multiplying out the right side and checking it equals the left side.
To test a claimed identity, try simple values. If even one value fails, it is NOT an identity; passing a few tests suggests (but does not prove) it is one.

example.q: If a + b + c = 15 and ab + bc + ca = 74, find a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc.

learn.reallife: Software testers do the same as you: one failing case proves a program (or an identity) is wrong.

games.title: Identity or not?
items: (a + b)² = a² + b² for all a, b
a = b = 1 gives 4 ≠ 2.
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
Multiplying out gives a³ + b³.
(a − b)² = (b − a)²
Both equal a² − 2ab + b².
(a + b)³ = a³ + b³
a = b = 1 gives 8 ≠ 2.
a² − b² = (a − b)²
a = 3, b = 1 gives 8 ≠ 4.

quiz.q: Factorise x³ + 125.
quiz.explain: Use a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) with b = 5.
steps: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) with b = 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses + ab in the second bracket, which belongs to a³ − b³

quiz.q: Use the sum of cubes to find 8³ + 2³ as (a + b)(a² − ab + b²).
quiz.mistake: Cubes the sum: (8 + 2)³

quiz.q: Using x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx), find the value for x = 1, y = 2, z = 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the −3xyz term

quiz.q: If a + b + c = 12 and ab + bc + ca = 47, what is a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc?
quiz.mistake: Stops after finding the second bracket, or multiplies 12 by 47

quiz.q: Riya checks (a + b)² = a² + b² + 2 using a = 1, b = 1 and finds both sides equal 4. What can she conclude?
options: Nothing yet; she must test other values, and a = 2, b = 1 shows it fails
It is an identity for all whole numbers
quiz.explain: With a = 2, b = 1: 9 versus 4 + 1 + 2 = 7. One value that works does not prove an identity.
steps: One value that works does not prove an identity.
9 ≠ 7, so it is not an identity.
Answer: Nothing yet; she must test other values, and a = 2, b = 1 shows it fails
quiz.mistake: Thinks one successful test proves an identity

quiz.q: Which value shows that (x + 1)² = x² + 1 is not an identity?
quiz.explain: x = 1: left 4, right 2. (x = 0 gives 1 = 1, which hides the error.)
steps: x = 0: left (0 + 1)² = 1, right 0 + 1 = 1 (equal, hides the error).
quiz.mistake: Tests only x = 0

quiz.q: To verify a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), you multiply out the right side. Which terms cancel?
quiz.explain: (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) = a³ + a²b + ab² − a²b − ab² − b³ = a³ − b³.
steps: (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) = a³ + a²b + ab² − a²b − ab² − b³.
What is left is a³ − b³.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cubes cancel

quiz.q: If a + b + c = 6 and ab + bc + ca = 11, find a² + b² + c².
steps: a² + b² + c² = (a + b + c)² − 2(ab + bc + ca).
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the pairwise sum

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I know if something is really an identity?"
teach.praise: Great thinking! It must work for every value; one failure busts it!
teach.nudge: Does an identity work for some values or all values? What does one failing value tell you?

revise.summary: x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz factorises with (x + y + z). Verify identities by expanding; test claims with values, since one failure disproves an identity.
focus: Use the three-cube identity with given sums.
Verify identities by expanding.
Disprove false identities with a counter-example.
remember: x² + y² + z² = (x + y + z)² − 2(xy + yz + zx).
One failing value shows it is not an identity.
traps: One successful test does not prove an identity.
x = 0 can hide an error; try other values.
Double the pairwise sum when finding x² + y² + z².

learn.hook: Factorising can be done with your hands: arrange tiles into a perfect rectangle and read off the sides!
points: Algebra tiles: a big square of side x has area x², a long strip x by 1 has area x, and a small unit square has area 1.
To factor x² + 7x + 12, take 1 big square, 7 strips and 12 unit squares, and arrange them into a rectangle.
The rectangle's sides are the factors: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4). The units form a 3 × 4 block and the strips split 3 and 4.
A path around a square ground of side x and width w covers (x + 2w)² − x² = 4wx + 4w²; tiles show the four strips and four corner squares.

example.q: Factor x² + 5x + 6 with tiles.
steps: Units arranged 2 × 3; strips 2 on one side, 3 on the other

learn.reallife: A gardener laying a paved border around a square lawn can count the paving stones the same way.

games.title: Build x² + 6x + 8
items: Place the x² tile
Find two numbers with product 8 and sum 6: 2 and 4
Put 2 strips on one side and 4 on the other
Fill the corner with 2 × 4 = 8 unit squares
Read the sides: (x + 2)(x + 4)

quiz.q: Which tile has area x?
options: A strip of length x and width 1
A strip of length 1 and width 1/x
steps: Area of a tile = length × width.
A strip x by 1 has area x × 1 = x.
The big square has area x²; the small square has area 1.
Answer: A strip of length x and width 1
quiz.mistake: Confuses the strip with the big square

quiz.q: How many unit squares are needed to show x² + 9x + 14?
quiz.explain: The constant term 14 is the number of unit tiles.
steps: x² + 9x + 14: 1 big square, 9 strips, 14 unit squares.
The constant term gives the number of unit squares.
quiz.mistake: Uses the coefficient of x

quiz.q: Tiles for x² + 9x + 14 make a rectangle. What are its sides?
steps: Need two numbers with product 14 and sum 9.
quiz.mistake: Uses the coefficients directly as the sides

quiz.q: Rohan arranges 1 x²-tile, 6 strips and 9 units into a square. What is its side?
quiz.explain: x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)², so the rectangle is a square.
steps: Equal sides make a square of side x + 3.
quiz.mistake: Takes the number of strips as the side

quiz.q: With 1 x²-tile, 5 strips and 4 units, which rectangle is possible?
quiz.explain: 1 × 4 = 4 and 1 + 4 = 5. (x + 2)(x + 2) would need only 4 strips.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the number of strips

quiz.q: A square park of side x m has a path 2 m wide all around it on the outside. What is the area of the path?
quiz.explain: Outer side x + 4. (x + 4)² − x² = 8x + 16.
quiz.mistake: Adds the width only once on each side

quiz.q: For the same path with x = 20, what is the path's area?
steps: Path of width 2 around a square of side x: (x + 4)² − x² = 8x + 16.
quiz.mistake: Gives the park's area instead of the path's

quiz.q: Why can x² + 3x + 5 not be made into a rectangle with whole tiles?
options: No two whole numbers have product 5 and sum 3
quiz.explain: 5 = 1 × 5 only, and 1 + 5 = 6, not 3.
steps: A rectangle needs two whole numbers with product 5 and sum 3.
So no rectangle can be made.
Answer: No two whole numbers have product 5 and sum 3
quiz.mistake: Thinks any set of tiles forms a rectangle

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can tiles help me factor x² + 7x + 12?"
teach.praise: Brilliant! Arrange the tiles into a rectangle and its sides are the factors!
teach.nudge: What shape do you make with the tiles? How do you read off the factors?

revise.summary: Algebra tiles (x², x and 1) can be arranged into a rectangle whose sides are the factors of a quadratic.
focus: Match tiles to the terms of a quadratic.
Factorise by arranging tiles into rectangles.
Find path areas with tiles.
remember: Big square = x², strip = x, unit square = 1.
Path of width w around side x: (x + 2w)² − x² = 4wx + 4w².
traps: The number of strips is not a side length.
Not every set of tiles makes a rectangle.
Add the path width on both sides.

learn.hook: 6x² + 7x − 3 looks scary, but find two numbers that multiply to −18 and add to 7, and it falls apart!
points: For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers with product a × c and sum b. Split bx using them, then group in pairs.
Example: 6x² + 7x − 3; a × c = −18, the numbers are 9 and −2: 6x² + 9x − 2x − 3 = 3x(2x + 3) − 1(2x + 3) = (3x − 1)(2x + 3).
For x² + px + q (a = 1) just find two numbers with product q and sum p: r² − r − 42 = (r − 7)(r + 6).
If (x − k) is a factor of a polynomial, then putting x = k makes it zero; this links its coefficients.
n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1), a product of three consecutive integers, so it is always divisible by 2 and by 3, hence by 6.

example.q: Factorise 2x² + 7x + 3.
steps: a × c = 6; numbers 6 and 1 add to 7

learn.reallife: Splitting things smartly into pairs is how quiz teams split prize money and how this method splits the middle term.

quiz.q: Factorise y² − 11y + 28.
quiz.explain: Product 28, sum −11: −4 and −7.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the sign of the middle term

quiz.q: Factorise 3x² + 10x + 8.
steps: a × c = 3 × 8 = 24; numbers with product 24 and sum 10: 6 and 4.
quiz.mistake: Checks the product but not the middle term

quiz.q: Factorise 6x² − x − 2.
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs of the factors swapped

quiz.q: To factor 4x² + 4x − 15, which two numbers should split 4x?
steps: a × c = 4 × (−15) = −60; the sum must be 4.
(5 and −3 have product −15, using c only.)
quiz.mistake: Uses the product c only, not a × c
Picks the number that matches the middle coefficient

quiz.q: (x − 2) and (x − 1/2) are both factors of px² + 5x + r. Substituting x = 2 and x = 1/2 gives 4p + 10 + r = 0 and p + 10 + 4r = 0. What follows?
quiz.explain: Subtract the second from the first: 3p − 3r = 0.
quiz.mistake: Adds the equations instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Using p = r in 4p + 10 + r = 0, what is p?
quiz.mistake: Drops the sign

quiz.q: Why is n³ − n always divisible by 6 for whole numbers n?
options: It equals (n − 1)n(n + 1), three consecutive numbers, so it has a factor 2 and a factor 3
quiz.explain: Among three consecutive integers one is a multiple of 3 and at least one is even.
steps: Three consecutive integers include a multiple of 3 and at least one even number.
So the product has factors 2 and 3, hence 6.
Answer: It equals (n − 1)n(n + 1), three consecutive numbers, so it has a factor 2 and a factor 3
quiz.mistake: Checks one example and calls it proof

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I factor 2x² + 7x + 3?"
teach.praise: Yes! Two numbers with product a × c and sum b, then split and group!
teach.nudge: Which two numbers do you look for? What do they multiply to and add to?

revise.summary: To factorise ax² + bx + c, find two numbers with product ac and sum b, split the middle term, then group.
focus: Split the middle term for a ≠ 1.
Factorise x² + px + q quickly.
Explain why n³ − n is divisible by 6.

Watch the signs of the two numbers.
Checking one example is not a proof.

learn.hook: Just as 12/18 cancels to 2/3, (x² − 9)/(x + 3) cancels to x − 3 — but watch out for x = −3!
points: A rational expression is a ratio of two polynomials, P(x)/Q(x), with Q(x) not the zero polynomial.
To simplify, factorise the numerator and the denominator fully, then cancel common factors (whole factors only, never single terms).
Values that make the denominator zero are not allowed. List them from the original denominator, before cancelling.

options: She cancelled a single term, not a common factor
quiz.explain: 4 is not a factor of the whole numerator x + 4, so it cannot be cancelled.

4 is a term of x + 4, not a factor of the whole numerator.

No, the original denominator is 0 at x = 3

Cancelling does not remove this restriction.

teach.praise: Excellent! Factorise, cancel common factors, and exclude values that make the denominator zero!

focus: Simplify rational expressions by factorising.
State values that are not allowed.
Avoid cancelling single terms.

chapters.title: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round

learn.hook: Tie a goat to a peg with a 5 m rope and let it graze: the edge of the grass it eats is a perfect circle!
points: A circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance (the radius r) from a fixed point (the centre O).
A chord joins two points of the circle. A chord through the centre is a diameter, and diameter = 2 × radius.
A point P is inside the circle if OP < r, on it if OP = r, and outside if OP > r.
No chord is longer than a diameter: for a chord AB, AB ≤ OA + OB = 2r (triangle inequality), with equality only when AB passes through O.

example.q: A circle has centre O and radius 6 cm. Where are points P, Q, R with OP = 4 cm, OQ = 6 cm, OR = 7.5 cm?
example.answer: P inside, Q on, R outside

learn.reallife: A compass used in geometry works exactly by the definition: the needle is the centre and the pencil stays at a fixed distance.

games.title: Where is the point? (r = 5 cm)

OP = 5 cm
OP = 6 cm

games.title: Chord facts
items: Every diameter is a chord.
It joins two points of the circle.
Every chord is a diameter.
Only chords through the centre are diameters.
A chord of length 13 cm is possible in a circle of radius 6 cm.
The longest chord is 12 cm.
The centre is inside the circle.
Its distance from itself is 0 < r.
A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle.
That is its definition.

quiz.q: A circle has diameter 18 cm. What is its radius?
quiz.explain: Radius = diameter ÷ 2.
quiz.mistake: Doubles instead of halving

quiz.q: Which is the longest chord of a circle?
quiz.explain: The diameter passes through the centre and has length 2r, the maximum.
steps: For a chord AB, AB ≤ OA + OB = 2r.
Equality holds only when AB passes through O, i.e. a diameter.
A radius is not a chord.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a radius is a chord

quiz.q: A circle has radius 7 cm. Which chord length is impossible?
quiz.explain: The longest chord is the diameter, 14 cm.
steps: 15 cm > 14 cm, so it is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that chords cannot exceed the diameter

quiz.q: A circle has centre O and radius 4 cm. OP = 3.5 cm. Where is P?
steps: So P is inside the circle.

quiz.q: A goat is tied to a peg with a 6 m rope. Which describes the boundary of the area it can graze?
options: A circle of radius 6 m centred at the peg
quiz.explain: Every point at the end of the tight rope is 6 m from the peg.
steps: With the rope tight, the goat is always 6 m from the peg.
All points 6 m from a fixed point form a circle of radius 6 m.
Answer: A circle of radius 6 m centred at the peg
quiz.mistake: Uses the rope length as the diameter

quiz.q: Why can a chord AB never be longer than 2r?
options: Because AB ≤ OA + OB = r + r
Because chords never pass through O
quiz.explain: In triangle OAB, one side is less than the sum of the other two (or equal if O lies on AB).
steps: In triangle OAB, a side is at most the sum of the other two.
Answer: Because AB ≤ OA + OB = r + r
quiz.mistake: Cannot connect chord length with the triangle inequality

quiz.q: Point Q is 9 cm from the centre of a circle of diameter 18 cm. Where is Q?
quiz.explain: Radius = 9 cm and OQ = 9 cm.
steps: So Q is on the circle.
quiz.mistake: Compares OQ with the diameter

quiz.q: A wheel has spokes from the hub to the rim, each 35 cm. What is the wheel's diameter?
quiz.explain: Spokes are radii; diameter = 2 × 35.
steps: Each spoke runs from the hub (centre) to the rim: a radius of 35 cm.
quiz.mistake: Takes the spoke as the diameter

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "What is a chord, and which chord is the longest?"
teach.praise: Perfect! A chord joins two points on the circle and the diameter through the centre is the longest!
teach.nudge: What does a chord join? Which special chord passes through the centre?

revise.summary: A circle is all points at a fixed distance r from a centre O. A chord joins two points of the circle; the diameter (2r) is the longest chord.
focus: Use diameter = 2 × radius.
Decide if a point is inside, on or outside a circle.
Explain why no chord exceeds the diameter.
remember: Inside: OP < r; on: OP = r; outside: OP > r.
AB ≤ OA + OB = 2r, equal only for a diameter.
r = 6 cm: OP = 4 inside, OQ = 6 on, OR = 7.5 outside.

A radius is not a chord.
Don't double when asked for the radius.

learn.hook: How many different circles can pass through your pencil dot? Infinitely many!
points: Every line through the centre is a line of symmetry of a circle, so a circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry.
A circle also has rotational symmetry about its centre by every angle: turn it by 1°, 37° or 200° and it looks the same.
Through one point, infinitely many circles can be drawn. Through two points A and B, also infinitely many.
The centre of any circle through A and B is equally far from A and B, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
The smallest circle through A and B has AB as its diameter, so its radius is AB/2.

example.q: A and B are 10 cm apart. What is the radius of the smallest circle through both, and where is its centre?
steps: Centre must be on the perpendicular bisector of AB
Closest such point to A is the midpoint M
example.answer: 5 cm, centred at the midpoint of AB

learn.reallife: A wheel can be fitted any way round on its axle because of its rotational symmetry.

games.title: Symmetry check
items: A circle has exactly 4 lines of symmetry.
Every line through the centre works: infinitely many.
A circle looks the same after turning by any angle about its centre.
Rotational symmetry of every order.
Only one circle passes through two given points.
Infinitely many do; their centres lie on the perpendicular bisector.
The centre of a circle through A and B is equidistant from A and B.
Both are on the circle, so OA = OB = r.
A line not through the centre can be a line of symmetry of a circle.
Only lines through the centre are.

quiz.q: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
quiz.explain: Every line through the centre divides it into two mirror halves.
steps: Every line through the centre divides the circle into mirror halves.
There are infinitely many such lines.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the horizontal and vertical lines

quiz.q: Which line is a line of symmetry of a circle?
quiz.explain: Folding along any line through the centre makes the halves match.
steps: A line of symmetry must fold the circle onto itself.
Folding along any line through the centre matches the halves.
A chord not through the centre or a tangent does not.
Answer: Any line through its centre
quiz.mistake: Thinks every chord is a line of symmetry

quiz.q: By which angles can a circle be rotated about its centre and still look the same?
quiz.explain: A circle has rotational symmetry for all angles.
steps: Turning a circle about its centre by any angle gives the same circle.
So it has rotational symmetry for every angle.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a circle with a square

quiz.q: How many circles pass through two given points A and B?
quiz.explain: Any point on the perpendicular bisector of AB can be a centre.
steps: A centre O must have OA = OB.
Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB works.
That line has infinitely many points.
quiz.mistake: Thinks two points fix a circle

quiz.q: Where do the centres of all circles through A and B lie?
options: On the perpendicular bisector of AB
quiz.explain: The centre O must satisfy OA = OB.
steps: The centre O satisfies OA = OB.
Points equidistant from A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Answer: On the perpendicular bisector of AB
quiz.mistake: Thinks the centre lies on AB itself

quiz.q: P and Q are 14 cm apart. What is the radius of the smallest circle through both?
quiz.explain: The smallest circle has PQ as diameter.
steps: The smallest circle through P and Q has PQ as diameter.
quiz.mistake: Takes the distance as the radius

quiz.q: A circle through A and B has centre O on the perpendicular bisector, 12 cm from the midpoint M, with AB = 10 cm. What is its radius?
quiz.explain: OA² = OM² + MA² = 144 + 25.
quiz.mistake: Adds the lengths instead of using Pythagoras

quiz.q: Can a circle of radius 4 cm pass through two points 10 cm apart?
options: Yes, if the centre is on AB
No, circles cannot pass through two points
No, the largest possible distance between two points on it is 8 cm
quiz.explain: Two points on a circle are at most a diameter (8 cm) apart.
steps: Two points on a circle are at most a diameter apart.
10 cm > 8 cm, so it is impossible.
Answer: No, the largest possible distance between two points on it is 8 cm
quiz.mistake: Forgets the diameter limit

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Where can the centre be if a circle goes through points A and B?"
teach.praise: Excellent! On the perpendicular bisector of AB, and there are infinitely many such circles!
teach.nudge: How far must the centre be from A and from B? On which line are such points?

revise.summary: A circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry for every angle. Infinitely many circles pass through two points; their centres lie on the perpendicular bisector.
focus: Describe the symmetries of a circle.
Locate centres of circles through two points.
Find the smallest circle through two points.
remember: Every line through the centre is a line of symmetry.
Centres of circles through A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Smallest circle through A, B: diameter AB, radius AB/2.
traps: Not every chord is a line of symmetry.
Two points do not fix a single circle.
Two points on a circle are at most a diameter apart.

learn.hook: Three villages want one water tank equally far from all of them. Where should it go? At the circumcentre!
points: Through three non-collinear points there is exactly one circle: its centre is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet.
Through three collinear points there is no circle: the perpendicular bisectors are parallel and never meet.
This circle is the circumcircle of the triangle, and its centre is the circumcentre.
To construct it, draw the perpendicular bisectors of two sides; their meeting point O is the centre and OA is the radius.
The circumcentre is inside an acute triangle, at the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.

example.q: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Where is its circumcentre and what is the circumradius?

learn.reallife: Placing a mobile tower equally far from three towns uses the circumcentre of the triangle formed by them.

games.title: Construct a circumcircle
items: Draw triangle ABC
Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB
Draw the perpendicular bisector of BC
Mark their meeting point O
Draw the circle with centre O and radius OA

quiz.q: How many circles pass through three non-collinear points?
quiz.explain: The perpendicular bisectors meet at one point, giving one centre and one radius.
steps: Perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at exactly one point.
That gives one centre and one radius.
quiz.mistake: Confuses three points with two points

quiz.q: How many circles pass through three points on one straight line?
quiz.explain: The perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC are parallel, so there is no common centre.
steps: For collinear points, the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC are parallel.
Parallel lines never meet, so there is no centre.
quiz.mistake: Thinks three points always fix a circle

quiz.q: The circumcentre of a triangle is the meeting point of its:
quiz.explain: Each perpendicular bisector holds points equidistant from two vertices.
steps: The circumcentre is equidistant from all three vertices.
Points equidistant from two vertices lie on the perpendicular bisector of that side.
Answer: perpendicular bisectors of the sides
quiz.mistake: Confuses perpendicular bisectors with angle bisectors

quiz.q: Where is the circumcentre of an obtuse triangle?
quiz.explain: For an obtuse triangle the bisectors meet beyond the longest side.
steps: Circumcentre: inside an acute triangle, midpoint of the hypotenuse in a right triangle.
For an obtuse triangle it is outside, beyond the longest side.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the centre is always inside

quiz.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 26 cm. What is its circumradius?
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle.
steps: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle.
quiz.mistake: Takes the hypotenuse as the radius

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 9 cm and 12 cm. What is its circumradius?
quiz.explain: Hypotenuse = √(81 + 144) = 15, radius = 15/2.
quiz.mistake: Halves a leg instead of the hypotenuse

quiz.q: To construct a circumcircle, how many perpendicular bisectors must you draw at least?
quiz.explain: Two bisectors already meet at the centre; the third passes through the same point and is a check.
steps: Two perpendicular bisectors already meet at the centre.
The third passes through the same point and is only a check.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all three are needed

quiz.q: Three wells A, B, C form an acute triangle. A pump equally far from all three is placed at:
quiz.explain: Equal distance from three points means the circumcentre, which is inside for an acute triangle.
steps: Equally far from A, B and C means the circumcentre.
For an acute triangle, the circumcentre is inside.
A midpoint of AB is equidistant from only A and B.
Answer: the circumcentre, inside the triangle
quiz.mistake: Chooses a midpoint, which is only equidistant from two points

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the centre of the circle through the three corners of a triangle?"
teach.praise: Superb! Draw perpendicular bisectors of two sides; where they meet is the centre!
teach.nudge: Which special lines of the sides do you draw? What happens where they meet?

revise.summary: Exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points; its centre (circumcentre) is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet. No circle passes through three collinear points.
focus: Construct a circumcircle.
Locate the circumcentre for acute, right and obtuse triangles.
Find circumradius of a right triangle.
remember: Circumcentre = meeting point of perpendicular bisectors.
Acute: inside; right: midpoint of hypotenuse; obtuse: outside.
traps: Perpendicular bisectors, not angle bisectors.
Two bisectors are enough to find the centre.
The circumcentre is not always inside.

learn.hook: Cut equal-length chords in a round roti and the slices to the centre all have the same angle!
points: The angle subtended by chord AB at the centre is ∠AOB.
Triangle OAB is isosceles because OA = OB = r, so its base angles are equal.
Theorem: equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre. Proof: if AB = CD, then △OAB ≅ △OCD by SSS (OA = OC, OB = OD, AB = CD), so ∠AOB = ∠COD.
Converse: chords that subtend equal angles at the centre are equal. Proof: △OAB ≅ △OCD by SAS, so AB = CD.

example.q: Chord AB subtends 70° at centre O. Find ∠OAB.

learn.reallife: A bicycle wheel's spokes cut the rim into equal arcs because the central angles are equal.

games.title: Which congruence?
pairs: Equal chords give equal central angles
Equal central angles give equal chords

quiz.q: In a circle with centre O, AB = CD and ∠AOB = 48°. What is ∠COD?
quiz.explain: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre.
steps: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle

quiz.q: Which congruence rule proves that equal chords subtend equal central angles?
quiz.explain: OA = OC, OB = OD (radii) and AB = CD (given): three sides.
steps: In △OAB and △OCD: OA = OC, OB = OD (radii), AB = CD (given).
Three pairs of equal sides: SSS.
No angle is known at the start, so not SAS.
quiz.mistake: Picks SAS although no angle is known

quiz.q: ∠POQ = ∠ROS at the centre O. What can you say about chords PQ and RS?
quiz.explain: This is the converse: equal central angles give equal chords (by SAS).
steps: Converse: equal angles at the centre give equal chords.
△OPQ ≅ △ORS by SAS (two radii and the included angle).
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal angles make chords parallel

quiz.q: Chord AB subtends 100° at the centre O. What is ∠OAB?
quiz.explain: Triangle OAB is isosceles; base angles = (180 − 100)/2.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 90 instead of 180

quiz.q: A chord subtends 60° at the centre of a circle of radius 9 cm. How long is the chord?
quiz.explain: The triangle OAB has a 60° angle between equal sides, so it is equilateral.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the chord must be a diameter

quiz.q: Why is triangle OAB isosceles for any chord AB?
options: OA and OB are both radii
quiz.explain: Any two radii of the same circle are equal.
steps: OA and OB are both radii of the same circle.
Answer: OA and OB are both radii
quiz.mistake: Assumes extra facts about the chord

quiz.q: A regular pentagon's corners lie on a circle. What angle does each side subtend at the centre?
quiz.explain: Five equal chords share 360° equally.
steps: The 5 sides are equal chords, so they share 360° equally.
(108° is the interior angle of the pentagon, not the central angle.)
quiz.mistake: Uses the interior angle of the pentagon

quiz.q: Chords AB and CD subtend 70° and 85° at the centre. Which chord is longer?
quiz.explain: In the same circle, a larger central angle gives a longer chord.
steps: In the same circle, a larger central angle gives a longer chord.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the smaller angle gives the longer chord

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Why do equal chords make equal angles at the centre?"
teach.praise: Wonderful! Radii and the equal chords give congruent triangles by SSS, so the angles match!
teach.nudge: Which sides of the two triangles are equal? Which congruence rule fits?

revise.summary: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre (by SSS), and chords that subtend equal central angles are equal (by SAS).
focus: Use the equal chords–equal angles theorem and its converse.
Use the isosceles triangle OAB.
Find central angles of regular polygons.
remember: Regular pentagon side: 360° ÷ 5 = 72° at the centre.
traps: Use SSS for the theorem; SAS for the converse.
Subtract from 180°, not 90°.
A bigger central angle gives a longer chord, not a shorter one.

topics.title: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord

learn.hook: Fold a paper circle so a chord's ends meet: the fold goes straight through the centre!
points: Theorem: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord (△OAM ≅ △OBM by SSS, and the two angles at M are equal and add to 180°).
Converse: the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord (△OAM ≅ △OBM by RHS).
So the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre; two such bisectors locate the centre of a circle.
Parallel chords: their perpendiculars from O lie on one line. Find each distance with Pythagoras; the gap between the chords is the difference (same side of O) or the sum (opposite sides).

example.q: In a circle of radius 5 cm, parallel chords AB = 8 cm and CD = 6 cm lie on opposite sides of the centre. How far apart are they?

learn.reallife: Archaeologists find the size of a broken round pot by drawing two chords on a piece and crossing their perpendicular bisectors.

games.title: Perpendicular facts
items: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it.
This follows from RHS congruence.
The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre.
Every point on it is equidistant from the chord's ends.
A line from the centre to any point of a chord is perpendicular to it.
Only the line to the midpoint is.

It is the difference.

Both pass through O.

quiz.mistake: Thinks the angle depends on the chord length

quiz.q: Which congruence rule proves that the perpendicular from O bisects chord AB?
quiz.explain: Right angles at M, hypotenuses OA = OB, and common side OM.
steps: Hypotenuses OA = OB (radii); OM is common.
quiz.mistake: Uses SSS before knowing AM = MB

quiz.q: In a circle, the perpendicular from O meets chord PQ at N. If PN = 7 cm, what is PQ?
quiz.explain: N is the midpoint, so PQ = 2 × PN.
steps: The perpendicular from O bisects the chord, so N is the midpoint.
quiz.mistake: Thinks N divides PQ unequally

quiz.q: How can you find the centre of a circle drawn on paper?
options: Draw one diameter and take its end
Fold it in any direction once

quiz.explain: Each perpendicular bisector passes through the centre, so two of them pin it down.
steps: The perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre.
Draw two chords and their perpendicular bisectors.

quiz.q: A chord of length 16 cm is 6 cm from the centre. What is the radius?
