A paper cup's outcomes are not equally likely.
Strong feelings don't make a probability objective.

learn.hook: Toss a coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads. Toss it 1000 times and the share of heads creeps very close to one half. Let's see why!
points: Experimental (empirical) probability is found by actually doing an experiment many times.
P(E) = number of trials in which E happened ÷ total number of trials.
Different runs of the same experiment can give slightly different results.
As the number of trials grows, the experimental probability usually gets closer to the theoretical probability.
The experimental probabilities of all the outcomes add up to 1, so P(not E) = 1 − P(E).

example.q: Kabir tosses a coin 50 times and gets 28 heads. Find the experimental probability of heads and of tails.

learn.reallife: Weather offices say there is a 70% chance of rain because, on past days with similar conditions, it rained on about 70 out of 100 of them.

items.q: 36 of 120 students walk to school: P(walks)?

games.title: What do experiments tell us?
items: If you repeat an experiment, you always get exactly the same probability
Random results change from run to run, so the experimental probability can change too.
More trials usually give an experimental probability closer to the theoretical value
Over many trials the lucky and unlucky runs balance out.
An experimental probability of 0.4 means the event happened in 40% of the trials
Getting 7 heads in 10 tosses proves the coin is unfair
With so few tosses, 7 heads can happen by chance with a fair coin.
Experimental probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1
Every trial gives exactly one outcome, so the counts add up to the total number of trials.

quiz.q: A coin is tossed 200 times and shows heads 112 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
steps: P(head) = number of heads ÷ total tosses.
quiz.mistake: Uses the theoretical value 0.5 instead of the data

quiz.q: A die is rolled 60 times and a 6 appears 12 times. What is the experimental probability of getting a 6?
quiz.explain: P(6) = 12 ÷ 60 = 1/5. The theoretical value 1/6 is close but not the same.
steps: (Theoretical 1/6 is close but not the same.)
quiz.mistake: Writes the theoretical probability 1/6 instead of using the experiment's data

quiz.q: A shop checks 500 bulbs and finds 20 defective. What is the probability that a bulb picked at random is NOT defective?

quiz.q: Aisha rolled a die 30 times: 1 came 4 times, 2 came 6 times, 3 came 5 times, 4 came 3 times, 5 came 7 times and 6 came 5 times. What is the experimental probability of getting a 5?
quiz.explain: 5 came 7 times out of 30 rolls, so P(5) = 7/30.
quiz.mistake: Uses the theoretical 1/6, or divides by the other rolls (23)

quiz.q: Which statement about experimental probability is true?
options: It is always exactly equal to the theoretical probability
It can change when the experiment is repeated
quiz.explain: It comes from actual results, which vary from one run of trials to the next.
steps: Experimental probability comes from actual results.
Results vary from one run of trials to another.
It cannot exceed 1 and needs data.
Answer: It can change when the experiment is repeated
quiz.mistake: Thinks experimental and theoretical probability are always the same

quiz.q: From past records, the experimental probability of rain on a July day in a town is 0.35. What is the probability of no rain?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts wrongly or adds instead of subtracting

teach.ask: Gappu tossed a coin 10 times and got 7 heads: "So is the chance of heads 7/10 now? I thought it was 1/2!"
teach.praise: 7/10 is the experimental probability from your 10 trials. With many more tosses it should get closer to 1/2. Clever!
teach.nudge: How did you get 7/10? And what might happen if you tossed the coin 1000 times?

revise.summary: Experimental probability = trials where E happened ÷ total trials. It varies between runs and usually gets closer to the theoretical probability as trials grow.
focus: Find experimental probabilities from data.
Use P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
Compare with theoretical values.
traps: Use the data, not the theoretical 1/6 or 0.5.
Divide by the total trials.
Experimental and theoretical values are not always equal.

learn.hook: A factory cannot test every single pen it makes. So how does it know how many might be faulty? Probability makes the prediction!
points: Expected number of times an event happens = probability × number of trials.
P(not E) = 1 − P(E), because an event either happens or does not.
The probabilities of all the outcomes of an experiment add up to 1.
A prediction is a good estimate, not a promise: the real count may be a little more or less.
A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning.

example.q: A factory found 3 faulty pens in a sample of 150. About how many faulty pens should it expect in a batch of 2000?

learn.reallife: Insurance companies, doctors and weather forecasters all use probability from past data to plan for the future.

quiz.mistake: Uses the old count 12 without scaling to 25 balls

quiz.q: A spinner can stop on A, B or C. P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(C)?
quiz.explain: All probabilities add to 1, so P(C) = 1 − 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2.
quiz.mistake: Adds P(A) and P(B) and stops there

quiz.q: In a game with one die, Riya wins if it shows 6 and Arjun wins if it shows 1 to 5. Is the game fair?
options: No, Arjun's chance is 5/6 and Riya's is only 1/6
Yes, because a die is fair
quiz.explain: A fair game needs equal chances. Arjun has 5 winning outcomes and Riya has just 1.
steps: Unequal chances, so the game is not fair.
Answer: No, Arjun's chance is 5/6 and Riya's is only 1/6
quiz.mistake: Thinks a fair die automatically makes any game fair

quiz.q: Arjun tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. What can he conclude?
options: The next toss must be a tail
The coin may still be fair; 10 tosses are too few to be sure
P(head) for this coin is exactly 0.7 forever
quiz.explain: Small samples vary a lot. A fair coin can easily give 7 heads in 10 tosses. Many more tosses are needed to judge.
steps: 7 heads in 10 tosses can easily happen with a fair coin.
10 tosses are too few; the coin does not remember past tosses.
Answer: The coin may still be fair; 10 tosses are too few to be sure
quiz.mistake: Believes a short run of results proves something, or that a coin 'remembers' past tosses

quiz.q: A bag has 20 marbles. Kabir picks one, notes its colour and puts it back, 100 times. He gets red 30 times. About how many red marbles are in the bag?
quiz.explain: P(red) ≈ 30/100 = 0.3, so about 0.3 × 20 = 6 of the marbles are red.
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of red picks (30) instead of scaling to the 20 marbles

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: "If the chance of rain is 0.3, how many rainy days should I expect in 30 days? And is it guaranteed?"
teach.praise: Multiply 0.3 by 30 to expect about 9 rainy days, but it is an estimate, not a promise. I'll carry an umbrella anyway!
teach.nudge: How do you turn a probability into an expected number? Is the prediction certain?

revise.summary: Expected number = probability × number of trials. Probabilities of all outcomes add to 1. A game is fair when every player has the same chance.
focus: Predict counts from probabilities.
Find missing probabilities.
Decide if a game is fair.
remember: Expected = P × trials; 3 faulty in 150 → 40 in 2000.
Fair game: equal chances for all players.
traps: P(not E) is not the reciprocal of P(E).
A fair die does not make every game fair.
Short runs prove nothing; coins don't remember.

topics.title: Many trials, fair outcomes and the gambler's fallacy

learn.hook: Five heads in a row: is tails 'due' now? Nope! The coin has no memory!
points: Law of large numbers: with more and more trials, the experimental probability tends to get closer to the theoretical one.
Rolling a fair die 60 times may give 6 about 10 times, but maybe 7 or 14; in 6000 rolls the relative frequency is usually very close to 1/6.
Gambler's fallacy: believing that past results change future chances. Each toss of a fair coin is still 1/2 heads, even after 5 heads in a row.
Before using 'favourable ÷ total', check the outcomes are equally likely. 'Win, lose or draw' are three outcomes, but they are usually not equally likely, so P(win) is not automatically 1/3.

example.q: A fair die is rolled 600 times and shows 6 on 94 rolls. Compare experimental and theoretical probability.
steps: Close, and likely to get closer with more rolls

learn.reallife: Lottery players sometimes pick 'overdue' numbers, but every draw is a fresh start. That's the gambler's fallacy.

games.title: Chance myths
items: After 4 tails, the next toss is more likely to be heads.
Each toss is independent; still 1/2.
More rolls of a die usually bring the relative frequency of 6 closer to 1/6.
That is the law of large numbers.
Win, lose and draw are always equally likely.
They depend on the teams; not equally likely in general.
Odd and even on a fair die are equally likely.
Each has 3 of 6 faces.
A die rolled 60 times must show each number exactly 10 times.
Random results vary; 10 is only the expected count.

items.q: Fair die, 6000 rolls: expected odd numbers

quiz.q: A fair coin has shown heads 6 times in a row. What is the probability of heads on the next toss?
quiz.explain: The coin does not remember earlier tosses.
steps: A fair coin does not remember earlier tosses.
quiz.mistake: Believes tails is 'due' (gambler's fallacy)

quiz.q: Which is an example of the gambler's fallacy?
options: 'A fair die gives each number with chance 1/6'
'Number 3 hasn't come in 20 rolls, so it's due next'
'The coin is fair, so heads is 1/2'
quiz.explain: Past results do not make a number 'due'.
steps: Gambler's fallacy: thinking past results change future chances.
'3 is due' assumes a gap makes 3 more likely.
Answer: 'Number 3 hasn't come in 20 rolls, so it's due next'
quiz.mistake: Thinks long gaps change chances

quiz.q: Riya rolls a fair die 60 times and gets 6 on 15 rolls. Which is most reasonable?
options: Random variation; with thousands of rolls it would likely settle near 1/6
quiz.explain: 60 rolls is a small sample; 15 is possible by chance.
steps: Expected 6s in 60 rolls ≈ 10; 15 is possible by chance.
With thousands of rolls the relative frequency tends to 1/6.
Answer: Random variation; with thousands of rolls it would likely settle near 1/6
quiz.mistake: Draws strong conclusions from a small sample

quiz.q: A die is rolled 6000 times. About how many times should 2 appear?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 instead of 6

quiz.q: Which experiment's relative frequency is most likely to be close to the theoretical probability?
quiz.explain: More trials generally give results closer to the theory.
steps: Law of large numbers: more trials → closer to theory.
6000 is the largest number of trials.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fewer trials are more accurate

quiz.q: A football match can end in win, loss or draw for India. Why is P(win) not simply 1/3?
options: The three outcomes are not equally likely
quiz.explain: The formula needs equally likely outcomes; team strength changes the chances.
steps: Favourable ÷ total needs equally likely outcomes.
Win, loss and draw depend on team strength.
So they are not equally likely.
Answer: The three outcomes are not equally likely
quiz.mistake: Applies favourable ÷ total without checking equal likelihood

quiz.q: A spinner has sectors of 180°, 90° and 90° coloured red, blue and green. Are the colours equally likely?
options: No; red has probability 1/2, blue and green 1/4 each
Yes, because there are three colours
quiz.explain: Chance depends on the size of each sector, not the number of colours.
steps: Answer: No; red has probability 1/2, blue and green 1/4 each
quiz.mistake: Counts colours instead of comparing sector sizes

quiz.q: For a fair die, which pair of events is equally likely?
options: Getting a 6 and getting less than 6
Getting an odd number and getting an even number
quiz.explain: Odd {1, 3, 5} and even {2, 4, 6} each have 3 outcomes.
steps: The other pairs have 1 vs 5 or 3 vs 1 outcomes.
Answer: Getting an odd number and getting an even number
quiz.mistake: Thinks single numbers and groups are equally likely

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "After 5 heads in a row, isn't tails more likely now?"
teach.praise: Right! The coin has no memory; it's still 1/2 each time!
teach.nudge: Does the coin remember what happened before? What is the chance on every toss?

revise.summary: With more trials, experimental probability tends towards the theoretical value. Past results never change the chance of a fair coin or die. Favourable ÷ total needs equally likely outcomes.
focus: Explain the law of large numbers.
Spot the gambler's fallacy.
Check equal likelihood before using the formula.
traps: No outcome is ever 'due'.
Win, lose, draw are not automatically 1/3 each.
Count sector sizes, not colours.

learn.hook: A coin and a die together: how many different results? A tree diagram grows the answer branch by branch!
points: List the sample space carefully: one coin {H, T}; one die {1, ..., 6}; two coins {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
A coin with a die gives 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes: H1, H2, ..., T6. Two dice give 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes.
Menus and choices: 3 snacks and 2 drinks give 3 × 2 = 6 combinations.
A tree diagram shows multi-step experiments: each stage branches into its outcomes; the number of end branches is the size of the sample space.

example.q: Draw a tree for tossing a coin three times. How many outcomes, and what is P(exactly two heads)?

learn.reallife: A canteen offering 4 types of paratha and 3 chutneys can advertise 12 different combos!

quiz.q: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
quiz.explain: 2 outcomes × 6 outcomes.
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 + 6

quiz.q: For a coin and a die together, what is P(tails and a number greater than 4)?
quiz.explain: T5 and T6: 2 favourable out of 12 = 1/6.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one of T5, T6

quiz.q: Two dice are rolled. How many ways can the sum be 8?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that (2,6) and (6,2) are different

quiz.q: Two dice are rolled. What is P(sum = 8)?
quiz.explain: 5 favourable outcomes out of 36.
quiz.mistake: Uses the 11 possible sums as equally likely

quiz.q: A thali has a choice of 3 sabzis, 2 dals and 2 sweets. How many different thalis can be made?
quiz.mistake: Adds the choices

quiz.q: Three coins are tossed. What is P(at least one tail)?
quiz.explain: Only HHH has no tail: 1 − 1/8.
steps: No tail only in HHH: 1 outcome.
quiz.mistake: Counts 'exactly one tail'

quiz.q: In a tree diagram for two tosses of a coin, how many end branches are there?
quiz.explain: Each first branch splits into two: 2 × 2.
steps: Each splits into 2 for the second toss: 2 × 2 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Thinks HT and TH are the same

quiz.q: Kavya chooses a uniform: 2 shirts (white, blue) and 3 trousers (grey, black, navy). What is P(white shirt with black trousers) if she picks at random?
quiz.explain: One combination out of 2 × 3 = 6.
steps: White with black is 1 of them.
quiz.mistake: Adds the choices to get 5

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I list all outcomes when tossing a coin and rolling a die?"
teach.praise: Excellent! A tree or table shows 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes!
teach.nudge: How can you organise the outcomes? How many does each stage add?

revise.summary: List sample spaces carefully: a coin and a die give 12 outcomes, two dice give 36. Choices multiply, and tree diagrams show multi-step experiments.
focus: Count outcomes of combined experiments.
Use tree diagrams.
Find probabilities with two dice or three coins.
remember: Two coins: HH, HT, TH, TT.
Three coins: 8 outcomes; exactly two heads 3/8.
traps: HT and TH are different outcomes.
Multiply the choices; don't add them.
The 11 sums of two dice are not equally likely.

learn.hook: Put the sweet back or eat it? The answer changes your next chance!
points: With replacement, the object goes back, so the sample space is the same for every draw. Without replacement, it shrinks by one each draw.
Example: a bag of 3 red and 2 blue. Ordered draws of two: with replacement 5 × 5 = 25 outcomes; without replacement 5 × 4 = 20.
From a frequency table, P(outcome) = its frequency ÷ total. For spinners, use the fraction of the circle (angle ÷ 360°). For letter cards, count the letters.
Geometric probability: if a dart lands at a random point of a board, P(region) = area of region ÷ area of board.

example.q: A dart lands randomly on a square board of side 20 cm with a square target of side 10 cm in the middle. Find P(target).

learn.reallife: Lucky-draw organisers at a school fete decide whether to put tickets back after each draw: it changes everyone's chances.

Bag 3R 2B, without replacement: P(R then R)

quiz.q: A bag has 4 red and 1 green ball. A ball is drawn and NOT put back, then a second is drawn. How many ordered outcomes are there?
quiz.explain: 5 choices for the first and 4 for the second: 5 × 4.
steps: Without replacement: 5 choices for the first draw.
quiz.mistake: Uses 5 × 5 as if the ball were replaced

quiz.q: Same bag (4 red, 1 green), drawing two without replacement. What is P(both red)?
quiz.explain: Favourable ordered pairs: 4 × 3 = 12 out of 20.
steps: Both red: 4 choices first, then 3 red left: 4 × 3 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Uses with-replacement counting

quiz.q: Same bag, drawing two WITH replacement. What is P(both red)?
quiz.explain: 4 × 4 = 16 favourable out of 5 × 5 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Reduces the count as if without replacement

quiz.q: A survey of 50 families: 0 cars 12, 1 car 26, 2 cars 9, 3 or more 3. What is P(a family has exactly 1 car)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 100

quiz.q: The letters of the word MATHEMATICS are on 11 cards. One card is drawn. What is P(M)?
quiz.explain: M appears twice among 11 letters.
quiz.mistake: Counts M only once

quiz.q: A spinner has a blue sector of 135°. What is P(blue)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 180

quiz.q: A dartboard is a circle of radius 10 cm with a bullseye of radius 2 cm. A dart hits the board at random. What is P(bullseye)?
quiz.mistake: Compares radii instead of areas

quiz.q: A rectangular field 40 m × 25 m has a pond of area 100 m². A seed falls at a random spot. What is P(it falls in the pond)?
quiz.explain: Field area 1000 m²; 100 ÷ 1000.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of multiplying

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Does putting the ball back change the probability of the second draw?"
teach.praise: Yes! With replacement the bag stays the same; without it, the bag shrinks!
teach.nudge: How many balls are there for the second draw if you don't put the first back?

revise.summary: With replacement the sample space stays the same; without replacement it shrinks. Use frequency tables, spinner angles or areas to find probabilities.
focus: Count draws with and without replacement.
Find probabilities from tables, letters and spinners.
Use area for geometric probability.
remember: 3 red, 2 blue: with replacement 25 ordered outcomes; without 20.
Dartboard: P = region area ÷ board area; 400 board, 100 target → 1/4.
traps: Don't reduce the count when the ball is replaced.
Compare areas, not radii.
Count repeated letters each time.

chapters.title: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions

learn.hook: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... Indian poets studied this pattern of rhythms centuries ago, long before it got the name Fibonacci. Can you guess what comes next?
points: A sequence is a list of numbers in a definite order. Each number is a term: a₁ is the first term, a₂ the second, and aₙ the nth term.
A rule for the nth term lets you jump straight to any term. For aₙ = 3n + 2, the 10th term is 3 × 10 + 2 = 32.
A recursive rule builds each term from earlier ones, like the Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers: each term is the sum of the two before it.
Famous sequences: square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, ...; triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ...; cube numbers 1, 8, 27, 64, ...
Looking at the differences between terms often reveals the rule.

example.q: Find the next term of 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ... and a rule for the nth term.
steps: Differences: 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12

learn.reallife: Seat numbers in a stadium, the rows of dots in a rangoli and the beats in a tabla rhythm all follow sequences.

quiz.q: What is the next term of 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ...?
quiz.explain: The differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12: 30 + 12 = 42.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the last difference (10) the same, getting 40

quiz.explain: Each term is the sum of the two before it: 8 + 13 = 21.
steps: Rule: each term = sum of the two before it.
quiz.mistake: Adds a fixed number or doubles instead of adding the last two terms

quiz.q: The nth term of a sequence is aₙ = 3n + 2. What is the 10th term?
quiz.mistake: Writes 3 next to 10 instead of multiplying, or adds instead of multiplying

quiz.q: If aₙ = n² − 1, what is a₅?
quiz.mistake: Computes 2 × 5 − 1 instead of 5² − 1

quiz.q: The triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... What is the 7th triangular number?
quiz.explain: The nth triangular number is n(n + 1)/2. For n = 7: 7 × 8 ÷ 2 = 28. Or keep adding: 15 + 6 = 21, 21 + 7 = 28.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the 6th term (21)

quiz.q: A sequence starts with a₁ = 2, and each next term is twice the previous term plus 1. What is a₄?
quiz.mistake: Stops one step early and gives a₃ = 11

quiz.q: Which rule gives the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...?
steps: Check another rule: 3n + 1 gives 4 for n = 1, not 1.
quiz.mistake: Tests a rule on one term only instead of checking every term

quiz.q: Meena draws a rangoli with 1 dot in the first row, 3 in the second, 5 in the third and so on. How many dots are there in the first 6 rows altogether?
quiz.explain: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36. The sum of the first n odd numbers is always n².
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of dots in the 6th row (11) instead of the total

teach.ask: Gappu sees 3, 7, 11, 15, ...: "How can I know what the 50th number will be without writing them all?"
teach.praise: Find the pattern, write a rule using n, then put n = 50. No need to write fifty numbers!
teach.nudge: What is the same between one term and the next? Can you write that as a rule with n?

revise.summary: A sequence is an ordered list of terms a₁, a₂, ..., aₙ. A rule for aₙ gives any term directly; a recursive rule builds terms from earlier ones. Differences often reveal the rule.
focus: Find terms from an nth-term rule.
Use recursive rules.
Find rules from patterns and differences.
remember: Virahanka–Fibonacci: add the last two terms.
traps: Check a rule on every term, not just one.
n² is not 2n.
Differences can change; don't keep the last one fixed.

topics.title: Finite, infinite and partial sums; is it a term?

learn.hook: Is 100 in the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, ...? Don't list them all: let algebra check!
points: A finite sequence stops (the days of a week, 1 to 31); an infinite sequence goes on forever (all odd numbers), shown with '...'.
A partial sum Sₙ adds the first n terms: for 1, 3, 5, 7, ..., S₁ = 1, S₂ = 4, S₃ = 9.
To check if a number is a term, set the rule equal to it and solve for n. If n is a natural number, it is a term; otherwise it is not.
The solution n also tells you the position of the term.

example.q: Is 100 a term of tₙ = 4n − 1? Is 99?
steps: 4n − 1 = 100 gives n = 101/4 = 25.25: not a natural number, so no
example.answer: 100 is not a term; 99 is the 25th term

learn.reallife: A railway timetable lists a finite sequence of stations; the ticks of a clock form a sequence that goes on and on.

games.title: Finite or infinite?
items: Months of the year in order
All even numbers 2, 4, 6, ...
Roll numbers of your class
Pages of a book

quiz.q: Which sequence is finite?
options: The page numbers of a 200-page book
quiz.explain: It stops at 200.
steps: Page numbers of a 200-page book stop at 200.
Multiples of 5, halves and squares go on forever.
Answer: The page numbers of a 200-page book
quiz.mistake: Thinks any long list is infinite

quiz.q: For the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11, ..., what is the partial sum S₄?
steps: S₄ = sum of the first 4 terms.
quiz.mistake: Gives the 4th term instead of the sum

quiz.q: The partial sums of 1, 3, 5, 7, ... are 1, 4, 9, 16, ... What is S₁₀?
quiz.explain: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n².
steps: Sum of the first n odd numbers = n².
quiz.mistake: Gives the 10th odd number

quiz.q: Is 50 a term of tₙ = 3n + 2?
options: No, n is not a whole number
quiz.explain: 3n + 2 = 50 gives n = 16.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract 2 first

quiz.q: Is 75 a term of tₙ = 4n + 1?
options: No, n would be 18.5, not a natural number
steps: Answer: No, n would be 18.5, not a natural number
quiz.mistake: Rounds n to a whole number

quiz.q: Which term of tₙ = 7n − 4 is 66?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 4 instead of adding

quiz.q: For tₙ = n² + 1, is 50 a term?
quiz.explain: n² + 1 = 50 gives n² = 49, n = 7.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root

quiz.q: The sequence 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, ... is:
options: infinite, with terms getting closer to 0
quiz.explain: The '...' shows it continues forever; 1/n shrinks towards 0 but never reaches it.
steps: The '...' shows it never ends: infinite.
1/n gets smaller as n grows, closer and closer to 0.
Answer: infinite, with terms getting closer to 0
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sequence stops when terms get small

quiz.q: For tₙ = 2n + 3, what is S₃ = t₁ + t₂ + t₃?
quiz.explain: t₁ = 5, t₂ = 7, t₃ = 9; sum = 21.
quiz.mistake: Gives t₃ only

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can I check if 100 is in the sequence 4n − 1?"
teach.praise: Brilliant! Solve 4n − 1 = 100; if n is a natural number it's a term, otherwise not!
teach.nudge: What equation do you make? What kind of number must n be?

revise.summary: A sequence is finite if it stops and infinite if it goes on. A partial sum Sₙ adds the first n terms. To test if a number is a term, solve the rule for n and check that n is natural.
focus: Tell finite from infinite sequences.
Find partial sums.
Decide whether a number is a term.
remember: Odd numbers: S₁ = 1, S₂ = 4, S₃ = 9; Sₙ = n².
tₙ = 4n − 1: 99 is the 25th term; 100 is not a term.
traps: Don't round n to make it whole.
Sₙ is a sum, not the nth term.
1, 1/2, 1/3, ... is not finite: its terms get closer to 0 but never reach it.

topics.title: Recursive rules and the Virahanka numbers

learn.hook: How many ways can a drummer fill 5 beats with short (1-beat) and long (2-beat) strokes? Indian poets counted this more than 1200 years ago!
points: A recursive rule can use several previous terms. For example T₁ = T₂ = T₃ = 1 and Tₙ = Tₙ₋₁ + Tₙ₋₂ + Tₙ₋₃ gives 1, 1, 1, 3, 5, 9, 17, ...
Virahanka numbers: V₁ = 1, V₂ = 2 and Vₙ = Vₙ₋₁ + Vₙ₋₂, giving 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ...
Vₙ counts the rhythms of n beats made of short (1 beat) and long (2 beats) syllables: a rhythm of n beats ends in a short (leaving n − 1 beats) or a long (leaving n − 2 beats).

Virahanka (who lived some time between the 6th and 8th centuries CE) found them while studying Sanskrit poetic metres; Gopala (around 1135) and Hemachandra (around 1150) wrote about them before Fibonacci (1202). So they are often called Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers.

example.q: List all rhythms of 4 beats using S (1 beat) and L (2 beats).

learn.reallife: Tabla and mridangam players build rhythms from short and long strokes, the very patterns Virahanka counted.

games.title: Who and when?
pairs: Counted poetic rhythms, between the 6th and 8th centuries

quiz.q: What is the next Virahanka number after 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21?
quiz.mistake: Adds a fixed amount instead of the previous two terms

quiz.q: How many rhythms of 6 beats can be made from short (1 beat) and long (2 beats) syllables?
quiz.mistake: Stops one term early

quiz.q: Why is Vₙ = Vₙ₋₁ + Vₙ₋₂ for rhythms?
options: Because every rhythm has exactly two syllables
Each rhythm ends in a short (leaving n − 1 beats) or a long (leaving n − 2 beats)
quiz.explain: Splitting by the last syllable gives the two cases, which add up.
steps: Look at the last syllable of an n-beat rhythm.
Short last: the rest is an (n − 1)-beat rhythm. Long last: an (n − 2)-beat rhythm.
Answer: Each rhythm ends in a short (leaving n − 1 beats) or a long (leaving n − 2 beats)
quiz.mistake: Cannot connect the rule to the counting

quiz.q: Tₙ = Tₙ₋₁ + Tₙ₋₂ + Tₙ₋₃ with T₁ = T₂ = T₃ = 1. What is T₆?
quiz.mistake: Adds only the last two terms

quiz.q: A sequence has u₁ = 2, u₂ = 5 and uₙ = uₙ₋₁ − uₙ₋₂. What is u₄?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order

quiz.q: Who among these wrote about these numbers before Fibonacci?
quiz.explain: Hemachandra (about 1150) came before Fibonacci (1202); Virahanka and Gopala too.
steps: Hemachandra wrote about these numbers around 1150, earlier.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sequence was discovered in Europe first

quiz.q: Virahanka studied these numbers while working on:
quiz.explain: He counted the patterns of short and long syllables in verses.
steps: Virahanka counted patterns of short and long syllables.
That was the study of Sanskrit poetic metres.
Answer: the metres (rhythms) of Sanskrit poetry
quiz.mistake: Mixes it up with Fibonacci's rabbit problem

quiz.q: If V₁₀ = 89 and V₁₁ = 144, what is V₁₂?
quiz.mistake: Doubles the last term

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do you get the next Virahanka number?"
teach.praise: Yes! Add the two previous numbers!
teach.nudge: Which earlier terms do you use? What do you do with them?

revise.summary: Recursive rules can use several earlier terms. Virahanka numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... count rhythms of short and long syllables: Vₙ = Vₙ₋₁ + Vₙ₋₂. Indian scholars knew them before Fibonacci.
focus: Generate terms from recursive rules.
Count rhythms with short and long syllables.
Know the Indian history of these numbers.
remember: 4 beats: SSSS, SSL, SLS, LSS, LL = 5.
traps: Add the previous two terms, not a fixed amount.
Subtract in the order the rule says.
These numbers come from poetic metres, not rabbits, in Indian work.

learn.hook: Saving ₹10 more every week than the week before? Your savings make an arithmetic progression, growing by the same step every time!
points: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence in which each term is got by adding a fixed number d, called the common difference, to the previous term.
d = any term − the term before it. It can be positive, negative or zero.
The nth term of an AP with first term a is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
To find which term equals a given number, solve a + (n − 1)d = that number for n.
The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], or n/2 × (first term + last term).

topics.title: More about APs: recursion, two terms, multiples and graphs

learn.hook: An AP plotted on graph paper lines up as straight as a cricket pitch!
points: Recursive form of an AP: t₁ = a and tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + d.
From two terms: if t₃ = 11 and t₈ = 26, then 5d = 15, so d = 3 and a = 11 − 2 × 3 = 5.
Counting multiples: the 3-digit multiples of 7 are 105, 112, ..., 994, an AP with d = 7, so n = (994 − 105)/7 + 1 = 128.
Plotting (n, tₙ) for an AP gives points on a straight line, because tₙ = a + (n − 1)d = dn + (a − d) is a linear polynomial in n with slope d.

example.q: An AP has t₄ = 18 and t₁₀ = 42. Find a, d and t₂₀.

learn.reallife: Taxi fares that rise by the same amount each km form an AP, and their graph is a straight line.

revise.summary: An AP can be written recursively (tₙ = tₙ₋₁ + d) or found from two terms. Counting multiples uses the AP formula, and (n, tₙ) points lie on a straight line of slope d.
focus: Find a and d from two terms.
Count multiples in a range.
Write tₙ = dn + c and plot it.

The slope is d, not the first term.
Only APs give straight-line graphs.

learn.hook: Add 1 to 100 in ten seconds? Write the sum forwards and backwards, and every pair makes 101!
points: Write S = 1 + 2 + ... + n and also S = n + (n − 1) + ... + 1. Adding pairs, each pair is n + 1 and there are n pairs: 2S = n(n + 1). This idea appears in Aryabhata's work.
So Sₙ = n(n + 1)/2. Picture: two staircases of dots fit together into an n × (n + 1) rectangle.
The triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, ... are exactly n(n + 1)/2.
A block sum is a difference: 51 + 52 + ... + 100 = S₁₀₀ − S₅₀ = 5050 − 1275 = 3775.
To find the smallest n with Sₙ > target, test n(n + 1)/2 near √(2 × target). Some numbers are sums of consecutive numbers: 15 = 7 + 8 = 4 + 5 + 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.

example.q: Find the smallest n for which 1 + 2 + ... + n exceeds 300.

learn.reallife: Stacks of pipes or cricket balls in a triangle pyramid at a shop have 1, 2, 3, ... per row: the total is a triangular number.

9 as consecutive numbers: 4 + ___

Next: 2 + (n − 1) = n + 1; every column is the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the pairs sum to n

quiz.mistake: Stops at a sum less than 200

learn.hook: A king once promised a wise man 1 grain of rice on the first chessboard square, 2 on the next, 4 on the next... By the last square it was more rice than the whole world had!
points: A geometric progression (GP) is a sequence in which each term is got by multiplying the previous term by a fixed non-zero number r, called the common ratio.
r = any term ÷ the term before it.
The nth term of a GP with first term a is aₙ = a × r^(n − 1).
If r > 1 the terms grow very fast (doubling, tripling). If 0 < r < 1 they shrink, like a bouncing ball.
An AP grows by adding the same amount; a GP grows by multiplying by the same amount.

example.q: Find the 6th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ...

learn.reallife: Bacteria doubling every hour, a viral video being shared, and money growing with compound interest all follow geometric progressions.

games.title: GP true or false
items: In a GP, you multiply by the same number each time
That fixed multiplier is the common ratio r.
It adds 2 each time, so it is an AP. 4 ÷ 2 = 2 but 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.
The common ratio of 81, 27, 9, 3 is 1/3
27 ÷ 81 = 1/3, and every next ratio is also 1/3.
Starting from 1, the GP with r = 2 eventually overtakes the AP with d = 100
Doubling eventually beats adding a fixed amount. The 20th term of the GP is 2¹⁹ = 524288, while the AP's 20th term is only 1901.
The nth term of a GP is a × r × n
It is a × r^(n − 1), a power, not a product with n.

quiz.q: What is the common ratio of the GP 3, 12, 48, 192, ...?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts terms (12 − 3 = 9) as if it were an AP

quiz.q: What is the next term of 5, 10, 20, 40, ...?
quiz.explain: Each term is doubled: 40 × 2 = 80.
quiz.mistake: Adds the last difference (20) instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Find the 6th term of the GP 2, 6, 18, ...
quiz.mistake: Uses r⁴ (getting 162) or r⁶ (getting 1458)

quiz.q: Which of these is a GP?
quiz.explain: Each term is the previous one divided by 3, that is, multiplied by r = 1/3.
steps: A GP has a constant ratio.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a GP must be increasing

quiz.q: A lab starts with 50 bacteria, and the number doubles every hour. How many bacteria are there after 5 hours?
quiz.explain: After 5 doublings: 50 × 2⁵ = 50 × 32 = 1600.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 50 by 5 instead of doubling five times

quiz.q: What is the common ratio of 64, 32, 16, 8, ...?
quiz.explain: r = 32 ÷ 64 = 1/2. The terms halve each time.
quiz.mistake: Divides the earlier term by the later one, getting 2

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 81 m bounces back to 2/3 of its previous height each time. How high does it rise after the 3rd bounce?
quiz.explain: Heights: 81 × 2/3 = 54, then 36, then 24 m.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the 2nd bounce (36 m) or goes one too far (16 m)

quiz.q: Aisha sends a Diwali greeting to 3 friends. Each of them forwards it to 3 new people, and so on. How many new people receive it in round 5?
quiz.explain: Round 1: 3, round 2: 9, round 3: 27, round 4: 81, round 5: 243. That is 3⁵.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 3 × 5 instead of raising 3 to the power 5

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: "2, 4, 6, 8 and 2, 4, 8, 16 both start with 2, 4. Why is one an AP and the other a GP?"
teach.praise: In an AP you add the same number each time; in a GP you multiply by the same number each time. 2, 4, 6, 8 adds 2, but 2, 4, 8, 16 doubles!
teach.nudge: From 4 to the next term, did you add something or multiply by something?

revise.summary: A geometric progression multiplies by a fixed common ratio r each time. aₙ = a × r^(n − 1). GPs grow fast when r > 1 and shrink when 0 < r < 1.
focus: Find the common ratio.
Find the nth term.
Tell a GP from an AP.
remember: AP adds the same amount; GP multiplies by the same amount.
traps: Divide, don't subtract, to find r.
Use r^(n − 1), not rⁿ.
A GP can be decreasing.

learn.hook: Multiply by −2 each time and the sequence jumps back and forth across zero!
points: Recursive form of a GP: t₁ = a and tₙ = r × tₙ₋₁.
The ratio r can be greater than 1 (growth), between 0 and 1 (shrinking), negative (signs alternate) or even irrational, like √2: 1, √2, 2, 2√2, 4, ...
To test for a GP, check that each term ÷ the previous term gives the same r. To find which term equals k, solve a × rⁿ⁻¹ = k.
Three terms in a GP can be taken as a/r, a, ar. Their product is a³, which quickly gives a; then a sum condition gives r.

example.q: Three numbers in a GP have product 216 and sum 21. Find them.
steps: Take a/r, a, ar: product a³ = 216, so a = 6

learn.reallife: A savings scheme that doubles your money every 8 years makes a GP of amounts.

teach.nudge: What do you divide? What must be true about all the ratios?

revise.summary: A GP can be written as tₙ = r × tₙ₋₁. Its ratio can be negative or irrational. Three GP terms can be taken as a/r, a, ar, whose product is a³.

Find terms with negative or irrational ratios.

learn.hook: Zoom into a cauliflower floret and you see a tiny cauliflower. That's a fractal!
points: Sierpinski triangle: start with a shaded triangle, join the midpoints and remove the middle one; repeat in each shaded triangle.
After n steps there are 3ⁿ shaded triangles, and the shaded area is (3/4)ⁿ of the original: both are GPs.
Sierpinski carpet: split a square into 9 and remove the centre; repeat. After n steps there are 8ⁿ squares and the area left is (8/9)ⁿ, which gets closer and closer to 0.
Fractals in nature: tree branches, ferns, cauliflower and romanesco, snowflakes, river networks and coastlines repeat similar shapes at smaller scales.

example.q: After 3 steps of the Sierpinski triangle, how many shaded triangles are there and what fraction of the area is shaded?

learn.reallife: Designers use fractal patterns in rangoli, textiles and even mobile phone antennas.

topics.title: Graphs of GPs and the bouncing ball

learn.hook: Drop a ball from 16 m: it bounces to 8, then 4, then 2... Does it ever stop travelling?
points: Plotting (n, tₙ) for a GP gives points on a curve, not a straight line.
With r > 1 the curve shoots up faster and faster; with 0 < r < 1 it drops quickly and then flattens out towards 0.
Bouncing ball: if a ball dropped from height h bounces to r × the height each time, the bounce heights hr, hr², hr³, ... form a GP.

Total distance = first drop + 2 × (sum of bounce heights), because the ball goes up and comes down each bounce. For h = 16, r = 1/2: bounce heights 8 + 4 + 2 + ... approach 16, so the total approaches 16 + 32 = 48 m.

example.q: A ball is dropped from 16 m and bounces back to half its height each time. How far has it travelled when it hits the ground for the 3rd time?

learn.reallife: Sports scientists test cricket and tennis balls by measuring how high they bounce: a fixed bounce ratio gives a GP.
