learn.hook: Why list all divisors of both numbers when you could just count down and stop at the first one that works?
points: Improvement 1: check j = 1, 2, ..., min(m, n) only, and keep just the most recent j that divides both. At the end it is the gcd. No lists needed.
Improvement 2: search downwards from min(m, n) and stop at the first j that divides both; that j is the gcd.
Each refinement must still be correct: we must explain why it always gives the gcd (for example, no common divisor can exceed the smaller number).

Efficiency: these methods need up to min(m, n) checks, which grows with the VALUE of the numbers. For a 12-digit number that could be a trillion checks, while Euclid's method grows only with the number of DIGITS.

example.q: Find gcd(84, 36) by counting down from min(84, 36).

learn.reallife: Programmers improve slow apps the same way: first make it work, then make it faster while keeping it correct.

learn.hook: gcd(1000, 3) by subtracting 3 again and again takes over 300 steps. By division it takes just 2!
points: Subtraction method: gcd(m, n) = gcd(m − n, n) for m > n. Swap when m < n. Stop when one number becomes 0, since gcd(m, 0) = m.
When the numbers are very different, subtraction can take very many steps (like 1000 and 3).

Division method (Aryabhata used this repeated division in the kuttaka method of his Aryabhatiya, 499 CE, so it is called Aryabhata’s division algorithm): gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n), where m mod n is the remainder. Laid out like repeated long division: divide, then divide the divisor by the remainder, and so on, until the remainder is 0.
Why it works: if d divides m and n, it divides m − qn = remainder; and if d divides n and the remainder, it divides qn + remainder = m. So the common divisors (and the gcd) do not change.
The number of division steps grows with the number of digits, so it is very fast: it never needs more than about 5 times the number of digits of the smaller number.

example.q: Find gcd(1071, 462) by the division method.

learn.reallife: Encryption on your phone uses the division gcd algorithm many times a second because it is so fast.

quiz.explain: Keep subtracting the smaller from the larger (swapping as needed) until one number is 0.
steps: gcd(4, 12): swap so the larger is first → gcd(12, 4).
Answer: Swap to gcd(12, 4), then gcd(8, 4), gcd(4, 4), gcd(0, 4) = 4

quiz.mistake: Thinks it is fast only because of computers

learn.hook: The word 'algorithm' comes from a person's name. A Baghdad scholar who wrote about Indian numerals!
points: Al-Khwarizmi (9th century, Baghdad) wrote a book explaining the Indian decimal numerals and methods of calculating with them. Its Latin title began 'Algoritmi ...', and from his name came the word algorithm.
A prime number has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. So 1 is not prime (one divisor) and 4 is not prime (three divisors).
prime(n): compute divisors(n); if the list has exactly 2 elements, n is prime, otherwise it is not.
primedivisors(n): go through divisors(n) and keep only those d for which prime(d) is true. For 60: 2, 3, 5.

example.q: Use prime(n) to test 91.

learn.reallife: Your phone's security uses huge primes found by prime-testing algorithms far faster than listing divisors.

topics.title: Prime factorisation and gcd from factors

learn.hook: Every whole number above 1 is built from prime bricks. Record each brick and how many times it's used!
points: Prime factorisation algorithm: start with the smallest prime 2; while it divides n, divide and count; then move to the next prime. Record pairs (prime, power).
Example: 360 → divide by 2 three times (45), by 3 twice (5), by 5 once (1). Pairs: (2, 3), (3, 2), (5, 1), so 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
gcd from factorisations: take each prime common to both numbers with the smaller of its two powers, and multiply.
Example: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. Common primes 2 and 3: gcd = 2² × 3¹ = 12.

example.q: Find gcd(180, 252) from prime factorisations.

learn.reallife: Cryptographers depend on the fact that factorising very large numbers is extremely slow, even though multiplying primes is easy.

teach.praise: Superb! Take the common primes with their smaller powers and multiply!
teach.nudge: Which primes do you use? Which power of each do you take?

revise.summary: Prime factorisation divides by each prime as many times as possible and records (prime, power) pairs. The gcd is the product of common primes with their smaller powers.

topics.title: Tiling and the exact meaning of a quadrilateral

learn.hook: Floor tiles fit with no gaps and no overlaps. Which four-sided shapes can do that? Every parallelogram, for a start!
points: A tiling covers the plane with copies of a shape with no gaps and no overlaps.
Any parallelogram tiles the plane: two sets of equally spaced parallel lines (like sticks pinned in a grid) make rows of identical parallelograms.
A quadrilateral ABCD is made from four points A, B, C, D (no three on a line) and the four segments AB, BC, CD, DA, where the segments meet only at their ends.
A, B, C, D are vertices; AB, BC, CD, DA are sides; AC and BD are diagonals. AB and BC are adjacent sides; AB and CD are opposite sides; A and C are opposite vertices; ∠A and ∠C are opposite angles.
Name a quadrilateral by going round it in order: ABCD, BCDA or DCBA all name the same one, but ABDC is a different figure.

steps: Diagonals join opposite vertices: PR and QS
Opposite sides: PQ and RS (also QR and SP)

learn.reallife: Brick walls, chessboards and floor tiles are all tilings by parallelograms (rectangles and squares).

revise.summary: A tiling covers the plane with no gaps or overlaps; any parallelogram tiles. A quadrilateral ABCD is four points (no three collinear) joined in order by four sides that meet only at their ends.
focus: Identify sides, diagonals, opposite and adjacent parts.
Name quadrilaterals correctly.
Explain why parallelograms tile.
remember: Diagonals join opposite vertices: AC and BD.
ABCD = BCDA = DCBA, but ABDC is different.

learn.hook: An arrowhead has four sides, but one of its corners points inwards. Is it still a quadrilateral? Yes, a non-convex one!
points: Convex quadrilateral: every interior angle is less than 180° and the two diagonals cross inside it.
Non-convex (concave) quadrilateral: one interior angle is a reflex angle (more than 180°), like an arrowhead; one diagonal lies outside.
The interior angle at a vertex is the angle inside the figure; at the 'dent' of an arrowhead it is reflex. The four interior angles of any simple quadrilateral still add to 360°.

Other four-sided figures: self-intersecting (like a bow-tie, where two sides cross) and non-planar (the four points are not all in one plane, like a bent frame). A Venn diagram of 4-gons puts convex and non-convex quadrilaterals inside the bigger family of 4-gons.

example.q: An arrowhead quadrilateral has angles 30°, 40° and 30° at three vertices. Find the fourth angle and say what kind it is.

learn.reallife: The arrowhead shape is common in road signs and kites; its reflex angle points inwards.

learn.hook: Four sticks joined at the ends with pins can wiggle into many shapes. Engineers use this to build machines!
points: A four-bar linkage is a quadrilateral with fixed side lengths but movable joints; its angles change as it moves. It powers windscreen wipers, bicycle pedals with legs, and folding chairs.

Parallelogram linkages keep opposite sides parallel while moving: Watt's parallel motion guided steam-engine pistons; a pantograph copies a drawing larger or smaller; forces combine by the parallelogram rule.
Given 4 points with no three in a line, they can be joined into 3 different 4-gons (the vertex orders ABCD, ABDC, ACBD).

If the 4 points are corners of a convex shape, you get 1 convex quadrilateral and 2 self-intersecting 4-gons. If one point is inside the triangle of the other three, you get 3 non-convex quadrilaterals.

learn.hook: Kites in the Makar Sankranti sky, carrom boards and window panes are all quadrilaterals, but they belong to different branches of one big family!
points: A quadrilateral has 4 sides, 4 angles, 4 vertices and 2 diagonals. Its interior angles always add up to 360°, because a diagonal splits it into two triangles.
Trapezium: a pair of opposite sides parallel. Parallelogram: both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
Rectangle: a parallelogram with all angles 90°. Rhombus: a parallelogram with all sides equal. Square: both a rectangle and a rhombus.
Kite: two pairs of equal adjacent sides; its diagonals are perpendicular.
So every square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and every rectangle and rhombus is a parallelogram, but not the other way round.

example.q: The angles of a quadrilateral are x, x + 10°, x + 20° and x + 30°. Find all four angles.

learn.reallife: Engineers use parallelogram shapes in car jacks and folding gates, because they can change shape while opposite sides stay parallel.

revise.summary: A quadrilateral's angles add to 360°. Trapeziums, parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses, squares and kites form a family: every square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and these are parallelograms.

learn.hook: Push the top of a folding gate sideways: it leans, but opposite sides stay equal and parallel. That's the parallelogram's superpower!
points: A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles.
In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal.
Adjacent angles are supplementary: they add up to 180° (co-interior angles between parallel lines).
The diagonals bisect each other: they cut each other into two equal halves.

A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if any one of these holds: both pairs of opposite sides equal, both pairs of opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other, or one pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel. In a rectangle the diagonals are also equal; in a rhombus they are also perpendicular.

topics.title: Proving a quadrilateral is a parallelogram

learn.hook: Measure only the sides, or only the diagonals, and still be sure it's a parallelogram? Yes, with the right converse!
points: If both pairs of opposite sides are equal, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram. Proof: diagonal AC gives △ABC ≅ △CDA (SSS), so alternate angles are equal and the sides are parallel.

topics.title: Rhombus, rectangle and square: special conditions

learn.hook: Draw the four angle bisectors of any parallelogram and, like magic, they box in a rectangle!
points: If a diagonal of a parallelogram bisects one of its angles, the parallelogram is a rhombus (the diagonal makes an isosceles triangle, so adjacent sides are equal).
The bisectors of the four angles of a parallelogram form a rectangle: adjacent angles add to 180°, so their halves add to 90°, and each corner of the inner figure is a right angle.

Converses with extra conditions: a parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle; a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus; a parallelogram with equal and perpendicular diagonals is a square.
Without 'parallelogram' these fail: a kite has perpendicular diagonals but is not a rhombus; an isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals but is not a rectangle.

points: Proof of the midpoint theorem by construction: with D, E midpoints of AB, AC, extend DE to F with EF = DE. △ADE ≅ △CFE (SAS), so CF = AD = DB and CF ∥ AB. So DBCF is a parallelogram, giving DE ∥ BC and DF = BC, so DE = ½ BC.

learn.hook: Balance a cardboard triangle on a pencil tip. The balancing point is where the three medians meet!
points: A median joins a vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side. Every triangle has three medians.
The three medians are concurrent: they meet at one point G, the centroid (the balancing point).
Centroid theorem: G divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1 from the vertex, so AG = ⅔ AD and GD = ⅓ AD. (Proof idea: join the midpoints of two sides and use the midpoint theorem.)
Trisecting a segment AD: make AD a median of some triangle (pick B, extend BD to C with DC = BD). The centroid G is at one-third from D; the midpoint of AG gives the other trisection point.

topics.title: Varignon shapes and tiling with any quadrilateral

learn.hook: Even a lopsided, wonky quadrilateral can tile a whole floor. Spin it around its edge midpoints and watch!
points: Varignon parallelogram (midpoints of the sides joined in order): its sides are parallel to the diagonals and half as long.
If the original's diagonals are perpendicular, the Varignon figure is a rectangle; if they are equal, it is a rhombus; if they are equal and perpendicular, a square.

Tiling method 1: rotate a copy of the quadrilateral by 180° about the midpoint of one edge; keep doing this about edge midpoints. The four angles (sum 360°) meet at every vertex, and copies fill the plane.
Tiling method 2: the Varignon parallelograms of copies form a parallelogram grid, which shows how translated copies of the quadrilateral fit together.

example.q: A quadrilateral has diagonals 10 cm and 14 cm that are perpendicular. Describe its Varignon figure and its perimeter.
steps: Sides are half the diagonals: 5 cm and 7 cm
example.answer: A 5 cm by 7 cm rectangle, perimeter 24 cm

learn.reallife: Tile designers use 180° rotations about edge midpoints to make floor patterns with irregular shapes.

quiz.q: An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals. What is its Varignon figure?
quiz.explain: Each Varignon side is half a diagonal, so all four sides are equal.
steps: Each Varignon side is half a diagonal.
Equal diagonals make all four sides equal: a rhombus.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the equal-diagonal and perpendicular-diagonal cases

quiz.mistake: Uses the full diagonal as the side

steps: Each copy is turned by a half-turn about an edge midpoint.
quiz.mistake: Uses a quarter turn

quiz.q: Why do four copies of any quadrilateral fit around a point in such a tiling?
options: Its four angles add up to 360°

steps: The four angles of any quadrilateral add to 360°.
Each of the four angles appears once at the point, filling 360°.
Answer: Its four angles add up to 360°
quiz.mistake: Thinks only regular shapes fit around a point

steps: The Varignon parallelogram has half the area.

They are used only for triangles

quiz.explain: A parallelogram grid tiles the plane, guiding the placement of the copies.
steps: Varignon parallelograms of the copies join into a parallelogram grid.
That grid shows how translated copies of the quadrilateral fit.
Answer: They form a parallelogram grid showing how translated copies fit
quiz.mistake: Thinks Varignon figures are unrelated to tiling

teach.praise: Super! The kite's diagonals are perpendicular, so the midpoint figure is a rectangle!

Explain why any quadrilateral tiles.

topics.title: Which shapes tile? Pentagons, hats and bow-ties

learn.hook: Bathroom tiles are squares, honeycombs are hexagons, but you'll never see a floor of regular pentagons. Why?
points: Any triangle and any quadrilateral (even a non-convex one) can tile the plane.
A regular pentagon cannot: each angle is 108°, and 360 ÷ 108 is not a whole number, so copies cannot fill the space around a point.
Aperiodic tilings cover the plane but never repeat in a regular pattern. In 2023 a single shape nicknamed the 'hat' was found that tiles the plane only aperiodically.
Scissors congruence: a shape can be cut into pieces and rearranged. For example, joining the midpoints of a triangle's sides cuts it into 4 congruent triangles.
In a self-intersecting (bow-tie) 4-gon, the four vertex angles add up to less than 360°: they are 360° − 2θ, where θ is the angle where the sides cross.

example.q: Can regular hexagons tile the plane? Regular pentagons?
steps: Hexagon angle = 120°; 360 ÷ 120 = 3: yes, three meet at a point
So hexagons tile; pentagons do not

learn.reallife: Honeybees build hexagonal cells because hexagons tile without gaps and use little wax.

learn.hook: 2 samosas and 3 jalebis cost ₹110. How much is one samosa? There isn't just one answer, until you get more clues!
points: A linear equation in two variables can be written as ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a and b are not both zero.
A solution is an ordered pair (x, y) that makes the equation true. Example: (2, 3) is a solution of 2x + y = 7 because 4 + 3 = 7.
A linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions: choose any x, then work out y.
To check a pair, substitute both values and see whether the two sides are equal.
An equation like y = 3 can be written in two variables as 0·x + 1·y − 3 = 0.

example.q: Find three solutions of x + 2y = 8.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers mixing two kinds of sweets in a ₹500 box face a two-variable equation: many different mixes give the same total.

topics.title: Standard form, scaling and solutions in every quadrant

learn.hook: x/2 + y/3 = 1 and 3x + 2y = 6 look different, but they are the very same line!
points: To write an equation in standard form ax + by + c = 0, move every term to one side and clear fractions or decimals by multiplying by a suitable number.
Example: x/2 + y/3 = 1 → multiply by 6: 3x + 2y = 6 → 3x + 2y − 6 = 0, so a = 3, b = 2, c = −6.
Check that an equation really matches a situation by testing a simple case: if a pen costs ₹10 and a pencil ₹5, 'x pens and y pencils cost ₹80' is 10x + 5y = 80, not 10x + 5y = 80xy.
Multiplying an equation by any non-zero k gives the same solutions (the same line): 2x + y = 5 and 6x + 3y = 15 are equivalent.
Solutions can be in any quadrant: for x − y = 2, (5, 3) is in Quadrant I, (−1, −3) in III, and (1, −1) in IV.

example.q: Write 0.3x − 0.2y = 1.5 in standard form with integer coefficients.

learn.hook: Plot every solution of x + y = 5 and they line up perfectly, like students at assembly. One equation, one straight line!
points: The graph of a linear equation in two variables is a straight line. Every point on the line is a solution, and every solution is a point on the line.
To draw it, find two or three solutions, plot them and join them with a ruler.
x-intercept: put y = 0. y-intercept: put x = 0. These two points are often the easiest to plot.
x = a is a vertical line through (a, 0); y = b is a horizontal line through (0, b).
y = mx (with no constant term) always passes through the origin (0, 0).

learn.hook: A wheelchair ramp must rise only 1 cm for every 12 cm along. That 1 : 12 is its slope!
points: Slope (gradient) measures how steep a line is: slope = rise ÷ run = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
On a straight line, the slope is the same whichever two points you use.
Positive slope rises from left to right; negative slope falls; a horizontal line has slope 0; a vertical line has undefined slope (the run is 0).
Real life: ramps, ghats, ski slopes. A wheelchair ramp is recommended to have slope at most 1 : 12, so a 60 cm rise needs at least 7.2 m of run.
Using slope and one point: if the slope is 3 and the line passes through (1, 2), then the point with x = 4 has y = 2 + 3 × 3 = 11.

example.q: A line through (2, 5) has slope −2. Find y when x = 6.

learn.hook: Rewrite 2x + 3y = 6 as y = −(2/3)x + 2 and you can read the slope and where it hits the y-axis at a glance!
points: Slope-intercept form: y = mx + d, where m is the slope and d is the y-intercept (the line meets the y-axis at (0, d)).
From ax + by + c = 0 with b ≠ 0: y = −(a/b)x − c/b. So m = −a/b and d = −c/b.
Two different lines with the same slope are parallel: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 4.
Applications: a tank filling at 3 litres per minute holds y = 3x after x minutes (slope 3, intercept 0); Fahrenheit and Celsius are linked by F = (9/5)C + 32 (slope 9/5, intercept 32).

example.q: Find the slope and y-intercept of 4x − 2y + 6 = 0.

learn.reallife: An auto fare chart 'base ₹30 plus ₹15 per km' is y = 15x + 30: slope 15, intercept 30.

quiz.explain: The slope is the change in F per unit change in C.

learn.hook: One clue gives infinitely many answers. Add a second clue and, usually, just one answer is left. Two lines, one meeting point!
points: Two linear equations in the same two variables form a pair. A solution of the pair must satisfy both equations.
Graphically, the solution is the point where the two lines meet.
Lines that cross give exactly one solution. Parallel lines give no solution. Lines that lie on top of each other (the same line) give infinitely many solutions.
Substitution method: make one variable the subject in one equation and put it into the other.
Elimination method: add or subtract the equations (after multiplying if needed) to remove one variable.

learn.hook: Two apples and a banana weigh 500 g; one apple and a banana weigh 350 g. Take one picture from the other and an apple pops out!

topics.title: How many solutions? The ratio test

learn.hook: Without solving, can you tell if two lines cross, never meet, or are the same line? Compare the coefficient ratios!
points: For a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0:
If a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂, the lines cross: exactly one solution.
If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂, the lines are the same (coincident): infinitely many solutions. While solving, you get 0 = 0.
If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂, the lines are parallel: no solution. While solving, you get a false statement like 0 = 5.

To build a second equation for 2x + 3y = 6: for crossing lines change the ratio of x and y (x − y = 1); for parallel lines keep 2 : 3 but change the constant (4x + 6y = 5); for the same line multiply everything (4x + 6y = 12).

example.q: Decide the number of solutions of 3x − 2y = 5 and 6x − 4y = 9.

learn.reallife: Two trains on parallel tracks never meet; two roads that cross meet at exactly one junction.

steps: So every solution of one equation satisfies the other: the same line.
Answer: The equations describe the same line: infinitely many solutions
quiz.mistake: Thinks 0 = 0 means x = y = 0

So no pair satisfies both: the lines are parallel.

quiz.mistake: Reads it as a value of x

quiz.mistake: Matches the constants

quiz.q: Which equation, paired with 2x − 5y = 3, gives coincident lines?
steps: Coincident lines: one equation is a multiple of the other.
quiz.mistake: Scales only the left-hand side

quiz.q: Which equation, paired with x + 4y = 8, gives lines that cross at one point?
quiz.explain: 1/2 ≠ 4/(−1), so they intersect.
steps: The others keep the 1 : 4 ratio (parallel or the same).
quiz.mistake: Picks a scaled or parallel equation

teach.praise: Brilliant! Equal x- and y-ratios but a different constant ratio means parallel!

revise.summary: Compare ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂, c₁/c₂: unequal first two → one solution; all equal → same line; first two equal but not the third → parallel. 0 = 0 means infinitely many; 0 = 5 means none.

learn.hook: Over 1100 years ago, Mahaviracharya asked: what is the price of one citron and one wood-apple? Pairs of equations are that old!
points: Mahaviracharya (9th century) posed: 9 citrons and 7 wood-apples cost 107; 7 citrons and 9 wood-apples cost 101. Adding: 16(x + y) = 208, so x + y = 13; subtracting: 2(x − y) = 6, so x − y = 3. Citron 8, wood-apple 5.
Babylonian tablets, the Chinese 'Nine Chapters' (with a method like elimination) and Indian texts all solved such problems long ago.
Graphical method for word problems: write both equations, draw both lines carefully on graph paper, and read the meeting point. Then check it in both equations.
Comparing plans: two phone plans y = 200 + 2x and y = 50 + 5x meet where 200 + 2x = 50 + 5x, at x = 50. Below 50 units the second is cheaper; above 50, the first.

chapters.title: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume

topics.title: Surface versus space: cuboids in layers

learn.hook: A 1 × 1 × 8 stick of clay and a 2 × 2 × 2 cube use the same clay. Which needs more wrapping paper?
points: Every solid has a surface (measured as area, in square units) and takes up space (volume, in cubic units).
Volume as layers: stack thin layers each with the base area; volume = base area × height. For a cuboid that is l × w × h.
The same volume can have different surface areas: 1 × 1 × 8 and 2 × 2 × 2 both have volume 8, but surface areas 34 and 24. Compact shapes lose less heat and need less packaging.
If the three face areas of a cuboid are A₁ = lw, A₂ = wh, A₃ = hl, then A₁ × A₂ × A₃ = (lwh)², so V = √(A₁A₂A₃).

topics.title: Surface area of cuboids, cubes and cylinders

learn.hook: How much paper do you need to gift-wrap a box of sweets for Diwali? That is a surface area question!
points: Surface area is the total area of all the outer faces of a solid, measured in square units.
Cuboid (l × b × h): total surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl). The four walls of a room (lateral surface) = 2(l + b) × h.
Cube of edge a: total surface area = 6a²; lateral surface area = 4a².
Cylinder of radius r and height h: curved surface area = 2πrh; total surface area = 2πr(r + h).
Open shapes (a box without a lid, a pipe without ends) need only the faces that are really there.

example.q: A closed cylindrical tin has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. How much metal sheet is needed to make it? (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Painters charge by the square metre of wall, and tin factories order metal sheets by the surface area of the cans they make.

teach.praise: Find the area of every face and add them all up. For a box that is 2(lb + bh + hl). Wrapping done!

revise.summary: Surface area is the total outer area. Cuboid 2(lb + bh + hl), cube 6a², cylinder curved 2πrh and total 2πr(r + h). Open shapes need only the faces present.

Find lateral and curved areas.
Handle open boxes and pipes.

topics.title: Packing, painted cubes and integer boxes

learn.hook: Dip a 4 × 4 × 4 cube of small cubes in paint. How many small cubes have no paint at all? Only the hidden heart!
points: Packing: the number of small boxes a × b × c that fit (in the same orientation) in a box L × W × H is (L ÷ a) × (W ÷ b) × (H ÷ c), using whole numbers only.
Painted n × n × n cube cut into unit cubes: 3 faces painted: 8 (corners); 2 faces: 12(n − 2) (edges); 1 face: 6(n − 2)² (face centres); 0 faces: (n − 2)³ (inside).
Cuboids with whole-number edges and surface area S: solve lw + wh + hl = S/2. For S = 22 there are exactly two: 1 × 1 × 5 and 1 × 2 × 3.

example.q: A 5 × 5 × 5 painted cube is cut into unit cubes. Count the cubes with 2 faces painted and with none.

learn.reallife: Warehouse managers plan how many cartons fit on a truck using this packing calculation.

teach.praise: Right! The inner (n − 2) × (n − 2) × (n − 2) cube stays unpainted!
teach.nudge: Where are the unpainted cubes? How big is that hidden block?

topics.title: Cylinders: discs, ratios and percentage changes

learn.hook: Stack khakhras one on top of another and you've built a cylinder!
points: A right circular cylinder has two equal circular bases, every cross-section parallel to the base is the same circle, and its axis is perpendicular to the base.
Think of a cylinder as a stack of thin discs (like khakhras or coins): each has area πr², and the stack has height h, so V = πr²h.
Ratios: if the radius is multiplied by k, volume is multiplied by k² (height fixed); if the height is multiplied by k, volume is multiplied by k.
Percentage change: radius up 10% (× 1.1) makes volume × 1.21, a 21% increase. Curved surface area 2πrh grows by the same factor as r × h.

example.q: Cylinder A has radius 3 cm and height 8 cm; cylinder B has radius 6 cm and height 4 cm. Compare their volumes.
example.answer: B has twice the volume of A

learn.reallife: A stack of ₹10 coins is a cylinder; doubling the stack doubles the volume, but a coin twice as wide holds four times the metal.

games.title: Cylinder changes
items: Doubling the radius doubles the volume.
It multiplies the volume by 4.
Doubling the height doubles the volume.
V = πr²h is proportional to h.
A cylinder's cross-sections parallel to its base are all equal circles.
That is part of the definition.
A stack of coins approximates a cylinder.
Thin discs stacked up.
Increasing the radius by 10% increases the volume by 10%.
It increases by 21%.

One circular base and an apex
A curved surface with no flat faces
quiz.explain: That is the definition.
steps: A right circular cylinder has two equal circular bases.
Its axis is perpendicular to the bases.

Because it is a cone tripled

steps: A cylinder is a stack of thin discs.

topics.title: Volume of cylinders, cones and spheres

learn.hook: Fill a cone with water three times and pour it into a cylinder of the same base and height: it fills up exactly. Maths predicted it!
points: Volume is the space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units. 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, and 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Cuboid: V = l × b × h. Cube: V = a³.
Cylinder: V = πr²h (base area × height).
Cone: V = ⅓πr²h, exactly one third of a cylinder with the same base and height.
Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³. Hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr³. When a solid is melted and recast, its volume stays the same.

example.q: A cone-shaped heap of wheat has radius 7 m and height 3 m. Find its volume. (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Water tankers, LPG cylinders, ice-cream cones and gol gappas all have volumes that companies calculate with these formulas.

quiz.q: A metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius 2 cm. How many small spheres are made?

quiz.mistake: Divides the radii (3) or compares areas (9) instead of volumes

revise.summary: Volume is the space a solid fills. Cylinder πr²h, cone ⅓πr²h, sphere (4/3)πr³, hemisphere (2/3)πr³. 1000 cm³ = 1 litre and recasting keeps volume the same.

topics.title: Cones: how they form and where we meet them

learn.hook: Spin a set square around one of its short edges really fast: the blur you see is a cone!
points: A right circular cone is formed by rotating a right triangle about one of its legs: that leg becomes the height h, the other leg the radius r, and the hypotenuse the slant height l.
Rotating the same triangle about the other leg gives a different cone (radius and height swap).
Problems: a birthday cap needs paper = curved surface πrl; a conical tent needs canvas πrl and holds air ⅓πr²h; a tarpaulin to cover a heap uses πrl.
A conical cup filled to half its depth holds only 1/8 of its full volume, because the water forms a smaller cone with half the radius and half the height: (½)² × ½ = 1/8.

example.q: A right triangle has legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the volume of the cone made by rotating it about the 8 cm leg. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: Ice-cream cones, traffic cones, mehndi cones and tent tops are all cones.

The other leg sweeps out the radius: 3 cm.

steps: At half depth, the water cone has half the radius and half the height.

topics.title: Surface area of cones and spheres

learn.hook: A birthday cap, an ice-cream cone and a cricket ball: two of these are cones and one is a sphere. How much material covers each?
points: A right circular cone has radius r, height h and slant height l, where l = √(r² + h²).
Curved surface area of a cone = πrl; total surface area = πr(l + r).
Surface area of a sphere of radius r = 4πr².
A hemisphere has curved surface area 2πr² and, with its flat circular face, total surface area 3πr².
If the radius of a sphere doubles, its surface area becomes 4 times as big.

example.q: A conical birthday cap has radius 7 cm and height 24 cm. How much paper is needed for it? (Use π = 22/7.)

learn.reallife: Tent-makers measure canvas for conical tents with πrl, and football manufacturers need 4πr² of leather for each ball.

l = √(r² + h²), which is more than h whenever r > 0.

learn.hook: The great pyramids of Egypt and the sharp peak of a temple tower share one formula!
points: A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces that meet at a point called the apex. Egyptian pyramids are square pyramids; mountain peaks and some temple roofs look pyramidal.
Volume of any pyramid = ⅓ × base area × height (height measured straight up from base to apex).
Surface area = base area + areas of all the triangular faces.
A cone is like a pyramid with a circular base: V = ⅓ × πr² × h follows the same rule.

quiz.explain: All side faces meet at the apex.
steps: All triangular side faces meet at one point.
Answer: The point where the triangular faces meet

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the volume of a pyramid?"
teach.praise: Perfect! One-third of base area times height!
teach.nudge: Which area do you use? What fraction of base × height is it?

revise.summary: A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at the apex. Volume = ⅓ × base area × height; surface area = base + all triangular faces.
focus: Find volumes of pyramids.
Find surface areas of square pyramids.
Link pyramids and cones.
remember: Base 6, height 4, slant 5: V = 48 m³, TSA = 96 m².
Pyramid = ⅓ of a prism with the same base and height.
Number of triangular faces = number of base sides.

learn.hook: Archimedes was so proud of this that he wanted it carved on his tomb: a sphere inside a cylinder!
points: A sphere is the set of all points in space at the same distance r from a centre.
Surface area = 4πr². Archimedes showed this equals the curved surface area of the cylinder that just encloses the sphere (radius r, height 2r): 2πr × 2r = 4πr².
Volume = (4/3)πr³, which is exactly 2/3 of the enclosing cylinder's volume πr² × 2r = 2πr³.

Hands-on: wind a string tightly over half a ball (a hemisphere), then use the same length of string to fill circles of the ball's radius. A whole ball needs string to fill exactly 4 such circles, so its surface is 4πr².

example.q: A ball has radius 7 cm. Find its surface area and volume. (π = 22/7)

learn.reallife: Cricket balls, footballs and laddoos are close to spheres; makers use 4πr² for leather and (4/3)πr³ for filling.

games.title: Archimedes check
items: A sphere's surface area equals the curved surface of its enclosing cylinder.
Both are 4πr².
A sphere's volume is half that of its enclosing cylinder.
It is two-thirds.
The string on a ball fills 4 circles of the ball's radius.
That gives 4πr².
Every point on a sphere is the same distance from its centre.
That is the definition.
The enclosing cylinder of a sphere has height r.
Its height is 2r.

quiz.q: What is the surface area of a sphere of radius 3.5 cm? (π = 22/7)

quiz.explain: The cylinder's height equals the sphere's diameter.
steps: A sphere fits snugly when the cylinder's height = diameter.

quiz.explain: 2πr × 2r.

quiz.mistake: Forgets the 4/3

quiz.explain: Surface area = 4πr² = 4 circles of area πr².
steps: That is 4 circles of area πr².

quiz.q: What fraction of a cylinder's volume does a sphere fill if it just fits inside?
quiz.mistake: Confuses with a cone's 1/3

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "What did Archimedes discover about a sphere in a cylinder?"
teach.praise: Wow! Same surface area as the cylinder's curved side, and two-thirds of its volume!
teach.nudge: Compare the sphere's surface with the cylinder's curved surface. What fraction of the volume?

revise.summary: A sphere's surface 4πr² equals the curved surface of its enclosing cylinder, and its volume (4/3)πr³ is 2/3 of that cylinder's volume, as Archimedes found.
focus: Find surface area and volume of spheres.
Use Archimedes' sphere–cylinder results.
Explain the string activity.
remember: Sphere = ⅔ of the cylinder's volume.
traps: Use the radius, not the diameter.
Cylinder height is 2r, not r.
Sphere is ⅔ of the cylinder, not ⅓.

topics.title: Maps, growing balls and hemisphere problems

learn.hook: On many world maps Greenland looks as big as Africa. In reality Africa is about 14 times bigger!
points: A cylindrical map projection wraps a cylinder around the globe and transfers the surface onto it. Near the equator it is fairly accurate, but near the poles the map gets badly distorted (on the common Mercator map, regions near the poles look much bigger than they really are).
If a sphere's radius is multiplied by k, its surface area is multiplied by k² and its volume by k³. A 10% larger radius gives 21% more area and 33.1% more volume.

Hemisphere problems: a dome's curved surface is 2πr² (for painting); a solid hemisphere's total surface is 3πr²; a hemispherical shell with outer radius R and inner radius r has volume (2/3)π(R³ − r³).

example.q: A hemispherical dome of radius 7 m is painted at ₹12 per m². Find the cost. (π = 22/7)

learn.reallife: Temple and mosque domes, gol gumbaz and planetarium roofs are hemispheres; painters estimate cost from 2πr².

games.title: Map and dome facts
items: Cylindrical map projections are most distorted near the poles.
The globe's surface is stretched most there to fit the cylinder.
On the Mercator map Greenland looks bigger than it really is compared to Africa.
Africa is about 14 times larger.
Painting a dome needs the area 3πr².
Only the curved part, 2πr², is painted.
A hemispherical shell's volume uses R³ − r³.
Outer minus inner hemisphere.
Doubling a ball's radius doubles its volume.
Volume becomes 8 times.

quiz.q: Why does Greenland look so large on many world maps?
options: The Mercator projection, a cylindrical map, stretches regions near the poles
The map uses a wrong scale everywhere
quiz.explain: Areas far from the equator get enlarged in such projections.
steps: The Mercator map is a cylindrical projection.
It stretches areas far from the equator, near the poles.
So Greenland looks far bigger than it is.
Answer: The Mercator projection, a cylindrical map, stretches regions near the poles
quiz.mistake: Believes the map shows true sizes

quiz.q: A ball's radius is doubled. How many times larger is its surface area?
quiz.explain: Area scales by k² = 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses k³

quiz.q: The inner surface of a hemispherical bowl of radius 14 cm is to be polished at ₹0.50 per cm². What is the cost? (π = 22/7)
quiz.mistake: Uses 3πr² for an open bowl

quiz.q: A hemispherical shell has outer radius 7 cm and inner radius 3.5 cm. What is the volume of material? (π = 22/7)
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the radii before cubing

quiz.q: A solid hemisphere has radius 7 cm. What is its total surface area? (π = 22/7)
quiz.mistake: Leaves out the flat face

quiz.q: The volume of a sphere becomes 27 times as large. What happened to its radius?
quiz.explain: k³ = 27 gives k = 3.
steps: Volume × k³ when the radius × k.
Answer: It became 3 times as large
quiz.mistake: Takes the square root instead of the cube root

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If a ball's radius doubles, what happens to its paint and its filling?"
teach.praise: Superb! Paint (area) goes up 4 times and filling (volume) 8 times!
teach.nudge: How does area depend on r? How does volume depend on r?

revise.summary: Cylindrical map projections distort areas near the poles. Scaling a sphere's radius by k multiplies area by k² and volume by k³. Hemisphere problems use 2πr², 3πr² and (2/3)π(R³ − r³).
focus: Apply k² and k³ to spheres.
Solve dome and shell problems.
Explain map distortion.
remember: Dome r = 7 at ₹12 per m²: 308 m², ₹3696.
traps: Use k² for area and k³ for volume.
Cube the radii before subtracting.
Use 2πr² for an open dome, 3πr² for a solid hemisphere.

learn.hook: How many golgappas does India eat in a day? Nobody counts, but you can make a smart guess!
points: Everyday objects match solids: a gas cylinder (cylinder), a laddoo (sphere), a matchbox (cuboid), an ice-cream cone (cone plus hemisphere). Use the matching formula to estimate volumes.
Units: 1 litre = 1000 cm³, 1 m³ = 1000 litres, 1 m² = 10,000 cm².
Guesstimation: make clear, reasonable assumptions, round numbers, and combine them to get a sensible estimate (often just to the nearest power of 10).
Different assumptions give different answers: the number of tennis balls in a room depends on the room size and how tightly they pack. State your assumptions.
Projects: water you drink in a lifetime (≈ 2 L a day × 365 × 70 years ≈ 51,000 L), ink in a pen, volume of your house.

example.q: Estimate the litres of water a person drinks in 70 years at 2 L a day.
steps: About 51 m³, enough to fill a small swimming pool

learn.reallife: Engineers planning a city's water supply start with exactly such guesstimates.

items.q: Water per year at 2 L a day (L)

quiz.q: How many cm² are in 3.5 m²?
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 as for length

quiz.q: A drum holds 0.2 m³. How many litres is that?
quiz.mistake: Uses 100

quiz.q: What is the first step of a good guesstimate?

quiz.mistake: Thinks estimation means random guessing

quiz.q: Two students estimate tennis balls in a classroom: one gets 30,000 and the other 60,000. Why can both be sensible?
options: They made different assumptions about room size or packing
One must have made an arithmetic error

steps: Estimates depend on assumptions about room size and packing.
Different assumptions give different but sensible answers.
Answer: They made different assumptions about room size or packing

quiz.mistake: Leaves out one factor

quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert m³ to litres

quiz.mistake: Squares the radius wrongly

teach.praise: Great thinking! Make clear assumptions, round numbers and combine them!
teach.nudge: What do you need to decide before calculating? Do you need exact numbers?

revise.summary: Everyday objects match solids, so their volumes can be estimated. Guesstimates state clear assumptions, round numbers and combine them; different assumptions can give different sensible answers.
focus: Match objects to solids and estimate volumes.
Convert between units.
Make and explain guesstimates.

2 L a day for 70 years ≈ 51,000 L.
traps: Use 10,000 for m² to cm², not 100.
Convert m³ to litres.
Estimation is not random guessing.

topics.title: The Earth-string puzzle and cube formulas

learn.hook: Tie a string around the Earth's equator, then add just 1 metre. Could a cat crawl under it? Surprisingly, yes!
points: Earth-string puzzle: circumference C = 2πR. Adding 1 m makes C + 1 = 2π(R + gap), so gap = 1/(2π) ≈ 0.16 m, about 16 cm.
The gap does not depend on R at all: the same 16 cm for a football, the Earth or the Sun.
For a cube of edge a: V = a³ and S = 6a². Since a = V^(1/3), S = 6V^(2/3).
Example: V = 64 cm³ gives a = 4 and S = 6 × 16 = 96 cm². Doubling the volume does not double the surface; it multiplies it by 2^(2/3) ≈ 1.59.

example.q: A string is wrapped tightly around a football (radius 11 cm). It is lengthened by 1 m. How big is the gap now?
steps: About 16 cm, the same as for the Earth

learn.reallife: Puzzles like this show why we trust algebra over gut feeling.

games.title: Puzzle facts
items: The gap from adding 1 m of string depends on the size of the ball.
It is always 1/(2π) m.
Adding 1 m of string around the Earth raises it about 16 cm.
S = 6V^(2/3) for a cube.
From S = 6a² and a = V^(1/3).
A cube of volume 27 has surface area 54.
Doubling a cube's volume doubles its surface area.
It multiplies it by about 1.59.

quiz.q: A string around a ball of radius R is lengthened by 2π metres. By how much does the gap grow?
quiz.explain: 2π = 2π × gap, so gap = 1 m.
steps: Extra length = 2π × gap (the radius terms cancel).
quiz.mistake: Thinks the gap depends on R

quiz.q: A string around the equator is lengthened by 1 m. About how high above the ground is it now? (π = 3.14)
steps: ≈ 16 cm, even for the whole Earth
quiz.mistake: Trusts the feeling that 1 m is tiny compared to the Earth

quiz.q: Does the gap in the Earth-string puzzle depend on the Earth's radius?
options: Yes, it is bigger for bigger balls
Yes, it is smaller for bigger balls
No, it is always 1/(2π) m for 1 m of extra string
quiz.explain: The R terms cancel: 2π(R + g) − 2πR = 2πg.
steps: R does not appear, so the gap does not depend on it.
Answer: No, it is always 1/(2π) m for 1 m of extra string
quiz.mistake: Thinks a bigger ball spreads the extra string thinner

quiz.q: A cube has volume 216 cm³. What is its surface area?
quiz.mistake: Uses S = 6V

quiz.q: A cube has surface area 384 cm². What is its volume?
quiz.mistake: Stops at a² = 64

quiz.q: Using S = 6V^(2/3), what is S for V = 343?
quiz.mistake: Uses V^(1/3) instead of V^(2/3)

quiz.q: A cube's volume is multiplied by 8. Its surface area is multiplied by:
quiz.explain: Edge × 2, so area × 4.
quiz.mistake: Assumes area changes like volume

quiz.q: A string is tight around a pole of radius 10 cm. To make a gap of 5 cm all round, how much extra string is needed? (π = 3.14)
quiz.explain: Extra = 2π × 5.
quiz.mistake: Adds just the gap

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If I add 1 m of string around the Earth, why is the gap the same as for a football?"
teach.praise: Mind-blowing but true! The extra length 1 = 2π × gap, and the radius cancels out!
teach.nudge: Write both circumferences. What happens to R when you subtract?

revise.summary: Adding 1 m to a string round any sphere lifts it by 1/(2π) ≈ 16 cm, whatever the size. For a cube, S = 6V^(2/3).
focus: Solve the Earth-string puzzle.
Move between a cube's volume and surface area.
Use scaling for cubes.
traps: The gap does not depend on the radius.
Area does not change like volume.
